Recently so many returns, some
of which are very voluminous, have been asked for, that they will just have to take their turn. They will be completed as quickly as possible. Every department is taxed to the uttermost.

The house resumed from Wednesday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Hon. R. J. Manion for the second reading of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific railway system, and for other purposes.

Mr. Speaker, during the course
of my remarks of yesterday in connection with the bill before the house, I pointed out that from 1929 to 1931 there had been a reduction of approximately 33,000 in the employees of the railroads of this country. This is not the only sacrifice that the transportation workers have made in connection with the present depression and the cooperative efforts that have already taken place on the part of the two railroads. We find that those employees have also accepted a considerable reduction in their hours and days of labour, and further, that they have taken a reduction in wages. This bill will, of course, further intensify the laying off and the possibility of a further reduction in the working days and hours of the men involved. We have come to the conclusion through a very practical experience that the individuals who go to make up the national life of this country are more important as consumers than as producers. It is not so very long ago that the whole drive was towards greater production. The cry was: Produce more and our problems will disappear. I think it will be agreed in view of the conditions in which we now find ourselves that that analysis was directly opposed to the forces at work in connection with the enormous productive capacity of the nation.
Rationalization both in the railways and in industry generally, unless its direct effect is to produce more employment opportunities for the men and women of this country, is not sound and should not take place in the economic structure and government of industry, where some people think it rightly belongs. In view of the very optimistic statements that were made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) in introducing this measure, more particularly that prosperity was in the offing, I am of the opinion that the tendencies towards consolidation should be slowed up. We should pause a while in the consolidation of our railway system lest we create a more intensified unemployment problem.
Coming to the question of amalgamation, I believe that there is still a great body of opinion in this country that thinks the real intent of this bill is amalgamation. I was glad to hear the minister say that such was not the case, but I was sorry to hear him and

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Mitchell
also the Prime Minister say that it was surplus language to include the section which was deleted from the original bill in the Senate reading:
But nothing herein shall be taken to authorize any amalgamation of any National company with any Pacific company.
I think tve have found that the laws of this country and possibly of every other country do not always work out as they were intended to, that the interpretation placed upon the legal phraseology after the passing of a law is quite often in direct conflict with the original intent of the lawmakers. I believe it would be well, Mr. Speaker, if that section were reintroduced into the bill so that the people of this country would have absolute confidence in the sincerity of the desire of hon. members of this house that this bill has absolutely no intent at this time, at all events of amalgamating the railroads of this country. I believe that it would allay the uneasiness in the public mind and definitely show the intent of this bill in regard to that question.
Coming to the board of trustees, the bill provides that a board of three shall be appointed. I should like to quote briefly from the observations contained in the memorandum of comments and recommendations on behalf of the railroad employees representing 200,000 workers:
We are particularly concerned about the problems involving the human element of the Canadian National and consider that at least one member of the new board of trustees, regardless of its size, should be especially qualified to counsel in respect to these problems because of his experience and the confidence imposed in him by the railway employees. This policy was recognized in the make-up of the present board of directors of the Canadian National, and also on other important public boards and committees. To this arrangement must be attributed much of the loyalty and enthusiasm, as well as good relations between management and men on the Canadian National of which the royal commission took special cognizance. In the opinion of railway labour it would be a grave mistake to ignore the wholesome lesson taught by this experience and in the face of it now deny labour the opportunity to continue to help in the administration of the government-owned railway system.
I agree with the contention of many hon. members who have spoken before me that it would be in the best interests of the Canadian National Railways if the board of trustees were increased to five. In view of the large reduction in the number of directors of the road, it must be conceded that the experiment we are making is revolutionary. I know of no example in this country either in business or in transportation where the
executive driving force has been reduced to so few in number. I believe it would be just as logical for the board of the Canadian National Railways to have a board of the same size as that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, because in that way you get the benefit of the various contacts and the various points of view, and I suppose that the directors are largely appointed for that reason. Of course, I am primarily concerned with the continuance of labour representation on the directorate of the Canadian National Railways. I agree with the Minister of Railways that without that loyal cooperation between the directors and employees and the magnificent esprit de corps displayed it would be practically impossible to run a large enterprise of this character successfully. The time has long since passed when labour should be expected to work merely for a daily wage. The logical course of events, and I believe it is the sound line to pursue, is that the best interests not only of the Canadian National Railways but of the Canadian Pacific Railway as well will be served only when the human point of view of the men and women engaged in that particular industry is reflected in the executive decisions that are made by the directorate. If such representation is not granted to labour on the board, Canadian railway labour will view i.t as a retrograde step. They anxiously look forward to the government of this country recognizing the soundness of their position, that no break should be made in the precedent which was established by a previous government in giving to the men and women engaged in the railway transportation business of this country representation on the board of directors.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that I have lost faith in big men. We have heard a lot recently about big men, the so-called supermen in this country. There is one thing for which the working people cannot be blamed; they cannot be blamed for present conditions because they were not consulted. I hope when the board is appointed better discretion, will be used by the government than has been used in the appointment of other commissions. I agree with the viewpoint of the hon. member for South Waterloo.
North Waterloo.

The hon. member will
not lose caste by accepting South Waterloo; however I thank him for the correction. In my view the board should be imbued with the spirit of service and a sympathetic inclination toward the soundness of public ownership.
Now I come to the arbitral tribunal. I believe that in this body too much power is

reposed in the hands of a single man, and I am convinced the objections taken are sound. Frankly I do not believe that the tribunal will be used to as, great an extent as some people imagine. I recognize the fact that some tribunal is necessary to act as a cushion between the conflicting viewpoints which might arise in connection with the cooperation which, in effect, is the principle behind the bill. I believe it is very necessary that some tribunal should exist to which the directors and management of the Canadian National Railways may go, and to which may be referred those matters upon which there have been expressions of public opinion. I am convinced however that the present Board of Railway Commissioners would have been a more satisfactory tribunal for that purpose, because they have as a background a wealth of information and experience in railroad matters. Further, they would be able to hear the evidence of parties who have not been heard in connection with this bill. The viewpoint of all communities affected should be heard. In fact, if necessary the viewpoint of the working men involved should be heard. For those reasons I believe the tribunal suggested in the bill is unnecessary, and would mean only further expense. I am convinced the work could be more expeditiously carried out by the railway commission, and that that body would be in a position to bring to bear more intelligent and practical opinions upon railway problems.
In conclusion I should like to express my views concerning the Canadian National Railways. I know that in certain sections of the press, and by some of the people of our country there is a tendency to look upon the national railways as the bad boy of public ownership. In this debate I believe it would be well to repeat that the Canadian National Railways were not the result of a deliberate policy of public ownership, but were the outcome of our mad rush to develop Canada. At the same time they offered a profitable investment for railroad promoters. Notwithstanding contrary opinions it is my view that the consolidation of the many roads under the control of the Canadian National Railways represents great progress, and is a monument to the genius for organization of Sir Henry Thornton. I predict I shall live to see the day when he will receive the credit he deserves in connection with this enormous undertaking. After all is said and done, the problems which confront our railroads are the problems confronting every industry and undertaking,-the problem of the elastic dollar. That problem is reflected in the fall in price levels, and in our inability to adjust
[Mr. Mitchell.l
our debt structure or to cope with the trade situation.
I am not unmindful of the great contributions the railroads have made to the development of Canada. That development is amply proven by statistics. We find that between the years 1900 and 1929 the mileage increased by 133 per cent, the gross earnings increased by 656 per cent and, incidentally, the external trade of Canada increased by 645 per cent. We cannot predict the future; this bill is based on the experience of the past. I believe that mighty tides are in the making which will carry this civilization either backwards or forwards. I hope we will have sense enough to let our imagination catch the flood of progress. Our railroads have been the arteries of our material development; we should see that our present conditions are only temporary.

Mr. Speaker, rising to say a few words concerning the bill before us, I find myself in a position very much similar to that described by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon). I cannot say I am supporting the bill because I have not any too much faith in what may arise from it. I do believe however, that if the trustees appointed under the bill are the type of men I should like to see appointed, in a very short time they will find themselves faced with a task so utterly impossible of solution that they will come back to parliament and recommend what parliament should have done when the railroads were consolidated in the first instance.
I do not intend to make more than a passing reference to what took place when the group of railroads which was found on the doorstep of Canada in the years 1916, 1917 and 1918 were brought into one common organization. But in view of statements which have been made concerning public ownership, what it has accomplished, what it may accomplish and all that sort of thing, and particularly in view of statements which have been made that the condition in which Canada has found herself during the last fifteen years with regard to railroads is due to the failure of private ownership, and to the building of railroads for the purpose, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, of providing profitable investments for promoters, I should like to make a very brief statement. The question of public ownership, as it could be applied to the Canadian National Railways, was never held out as an argument either for or against the principle of public ownership. Between the years 1900 and 1910 the parliament of Can-

C.N.R ,-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Nicholson
ada created a railroad situation-the parliament of Canada, not private owners, in any sense. It was the private owners who undertook to develop the railway lines in Canada, induced to do so by the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The owners of the Grand Trunk Railway made an effort to project their line into western Canada and practically came to an arrangement with the Canadian Northern interests by which the Grand Trunk in the east and the Canadian Northern in the west would comprise a transcontinental road. Then a transcontinental road was projected from Moncton to Brines Rupert and no arrangements were made to link up with the Grand Trunk. In this way a vast expenditure was loaded upon the transportation system of this country and the Canadian people are now in the position where they are called upon to carry that load.
In 1918 and 1919 parliament found it necessary to do something for these roads. At that time Canada had a total investment in these railroads of $1,106,237,629.72. There was a large surplus of mileage and if the problem had been taken hold of as it should have been taken hold of, this surplus would have been eliminated and the unnecessary capital which was wasted in the construction of the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific would have been written out of the picture and the railroads given a chance to carry on. But that was not done. The expenditure of
8300,000,000 would have brought these lines up to the standard of class one railroads, and anyone who wishes to read the debates which took place in the House of Commons during 1918, 1919 and 1920 will find the statements set out quite clearly. Any railroad man looking over the situation as it was then and as it is now will agree with that estimate of the amount required to bring these railroads up to class one condition. If the proper course had been followed that amount would have been sufficient. In the meantime, what have we done? We have raised our total liabilities from $1,100,000,000 to $2,600,000,000 and that is a burden the Canadian people have to bear to-day. People will say: What are you going to do, are you going to scrap portions of these roads after having paid for their construction? They will ask what is to be done with the territories through which they run. I say without hesitation that until the people of Canada acting through this parliament decide to abandon the surplus duplicating lines of the Canadian National Railway and, in many cases, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the railroad problem of this country will never be solved. I believe that if the right type of trustees are appointed they will find the task
so utterly hopeless even with cooperation that they will come back to this house and recommend to be done what we ourselves should have done long ago.
I should like to refer to some of the statements made with regard to the situation that has developed from 1920 on. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan), with whom I agree in some of the positions he has taken, stated yesterday that in 1923 Sir Henry Thornton found these railroads in the mud but had brought them up to the level of first class roads and only because of that was it possible to make the economies which have been made in operating expenses during the past year or two. When we look into what Sir Henry Thornton did say with regard to that I think it will be found that he agreed with the statement I made a few moments ago, that the cost of bringing these railroads up to class one standard was not $1,000,000,000 but $300,000,000. In 1922 Sir Henry Thornton made a statement to the Minister of Railways which appears on page 10 of the annual report of that year. After dealing with the general condition of the property, he said:
On behalf of the board, I would like to state that after inspection of the main arteries of the system, we find that the work undertaken has been well performed, and that the expenditures have been well applied. While the demands for capital expenditure on a system of such extent in a growing country, as the former board stated, are never ending, yet it may now be said that the three groups of lines, until recently the Canadian National Railways, enter the consolidation in excellent physical condition and operating at a high mark of efficiency as regards actual performance or movement of traffic and other factors controllable by management. Apart from certain well known cases of duplication the lines are well located and in exceptional position to successfully perform the transportation demands of the country. The problem as far as the lines covered by the report is concerned, is how sufficient traffic may be developed to carry the overhead and maintenance expenses. As far as transportation costs gO, an economical performance is being made. Under these circumstances the margin for improvement with the present light volume of traffic is largely dependent on circumstances beyond the control of the management.	,
On some of the older sections there are still improvements that should be undertaken, but in the main the lines are modern in character and were built or have been brought up to standards which are ahead of actual traffic requirements, except under stress of seasonal movements.
That was the statement made in 1922 by Sir Henry Thornton when he took over control of the property. It has been stated this afternoon as well as previously that some day a monument will be erected to Sir Henry Thornton. It is not my intention to find

! should like to ask one question for information. Is the hon. member taking into account in this summing up the contribution made by all the various branch lines to the earnings of the terminals of the system and a small part of the main lines themselves, which could not exist and earn anything without the branch lines?
* Mr. NICHOLSON: I was just coming to that. If you analyze the situation in relation to the Canadian National Railways or any other railway system you will find that the branch lines are given credit for the earnings which they contribute to the main line.
Perhaps.
They should be.

And they are, and in the analysis that has been made by the Duff commission you will find that this is how it
(Mr. Nicholson.]
is carried out. Each branch line is credited with the earnings originating on that branch line and also with the earnings originating on the main lines and projected to the branch lines. Everyone who knows anything about this country knows that in many cases branch lines have been projected ahead of their time, so to speak, but it is the duplication of main lines, of terminals and of services of every known kind that a railway must maintain if it is to operate which provides the difficulty.
I am sorry my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River has left the chamber; I wanted him to hear one or two things I have to say, because I am both in agreement and in disagreement with him. The hon. member referred to the consolidation of terminals and shops and so on and spoke of the effect this would have on the employment of labour. He particularly referred to what are known as back shops. Back shops, Mr. Speaker, are the shops where locomotives are taken when they receive what is known as a general repair, as contrasted to the ordinary running repairs from day to day which are looked after in the roundhouses. If you close the Angus shops of the Canadian Pacific Railway in Montreal and repair all the locomotives of both lines in the Point St. Charles shops of the Canadian National Railways, or vice versa, that will not necessarily mean that the mechanics who repair these locomotives will be dismissed. Not at all. A substantial saving will be made in fuel and in electric power and there will be some saving in supervision, but when these locomotives go in for a class A, a class B or a class C repair it takes the same number of mechanics to repair them in the Point St. Charles shops as it would take if the repairs were made in the Angus shops. The same thing, of course, applies to carshops. Certainly there will be some reduction in staffs, but in the main that reduction will not be in what are called mechanics but rather in the supervisory staffs of both companies. The same thing will apply in the yard service. You cannot switch a thousand cars with the same number of switchmen and switch engines as you can switch five hundred cars, I do not care whether you do it in one yard or in two.
This is the point, Mr. Speaker: Can the taxpayers of this country continue to carry this load, which is always increasing? The interest charge this very year will be increased by $2,500,000 or $3,000,000 by reason of the advances the country must make to cover the deficit and interest charges for 1932, and so on all along the line.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Nicholson
One other point raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was in relation to compensation. "What will you do," he said, "with the people located along these lines and with the railroad men who have gone into the terminals and built homes?" I fully agree with him that the country must compensate these men. At the same time I say to him that I can point out a thousand miles of railroad line in the province of Ontario where the rails could be taken up-and the roadbed turned into highways if you like-and every living soul on these lines evacuated, paid their expenses and put into some profitable employment somewhere else, and it will not cost this country more than an amount equal to the cost of maintaining the line for three years, without taking into account the operating cost. Certainly that is what we will have to face. The country must face it sooner or later, and my hon. friend is perfectly right when he says that compensation must be given. If this bill involves the abandonment of terminals or anything of that kind that brings hardship to individuals and groups who have gone there honestly or have been induced to go there, I say at once that the country should . compensate them without question.
There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer; that is what my hon. friend said with regard to statements that have been made in relation to the rates of pay and so on received by the running trades on the railways. My hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) referred to that point in his speech, I understand, although I did not hear it. There is a very considerable discussion going on throughout the country among men who do not understand, I think, what is the real situation with regard to the excess earnings of the running trades in railway service. These running trades, and the conditions under which they are employed, are frequently held up as the reason why the railroads are creating deficits instead of earning surpluses, as they should.
Only one of the reasons.

Well, as one of the
reasons. I submit, Mr. Speaker, and I believe I can show, that there is a very great misconception in the minds of a large number of people with regard to the basis upon which these men are employed. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was perfectly right when he said yesterday that these rates have not been fixed arbitrarily; they have been the subject of negotiation. It is true that the standard of living for railway employees has been materially raised during this century; it began to be raised about 1890, in relation to
other classes of working men. But this is the situation, and I will take 1928 as the basis for what I have to say, and I will refer to just one class of men employed in the running trades, the locomotive engineers, the highest paid class. In 1928 the basic rate of the locomotive engineer was not as high as the basic rate of a bricklayer, a plasterer, a plumber, an electrician or a carpenter in any city of this country. I challenge anyone to investigate the situation and find this out for himself. It is true, perhaps, that these men earn a day's pay in a few hours, but I am going to suggest this to anyone who has never tried it: Let any hon. member of this house get a pass from the Canadian Pacific Railway to-night-and a pass will be readily made available to him-and get on board one of those 2,300 class locomotives that pulls train number 5 out of here on the main line. Let him get into the most comfortable position that he can find in the cab of that locomotive and ride from here to Chalk River. When he gets there let him say whether he would like to turn right around and come back. I venture to say that he would want to go to bed and stay there all day to-morrow, and I know whereof I speak.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there is no class of labour in this country that is faced with greater responsibility and strain on their nervous and physical systems than the men employed in the running trades on our railroads. They are in control of machines that in themselves are so complicated that if a man had nothing else in the world to do but watch the variety of gauges with which he is faced in order to see that the train is kept moving along safely it would be enough to keep him busy, but that is not all the engineer has to do. I had hoped to have a standard rule book with me here. I should like to submit it to a group of lawyers in this house and find out how long it would take them to understand the rules and see what the man in charge of a train is faced with if he is to keep the passengers and the public safe. I venture to say it would take any man in the house a year thoroughly to understand those rules. It takes those men on the railroads much longer; they are apprenticed in the first place and gradually work up. What are they faced with then? There are all types and forms of signals, and complicated train orders are put into the hands of these men one or two minutes, never longer than that, before the train pulls out; and when a train is running at forty miles an hour we can well imagine what the possibilities are in the way of danger at one of the terminals with a

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Nicholson
myriad of lights flashing in the faces of the trainmen. If there is the slightest mistake on their part they are apt to run into the rear end of a passenger train and kill many people. One mistake and the doors of the penitentiary are open waiting for these men, and this because of the laws of the country. Let me give you one illustration. Less than a year ago a fast train of the Canadian Pacific, running between Smiths Falls and Trenton, and travelling at a speed of not less than seventy miles an hour, equipped with a series of lights in front of the locomotive, and an electric headlight, met with an accident through the detachment of this electric headlight. This occurred as the train approached the crossing. The engineer blew the whistle and did everything else he could think of, but an automobile was hit and a man killed. The engineer was arrested and thrown into prison. He was haled before the magistrate and committed for trial and put back into gaol, but his friends bailed him out and after a long period he was acquitted. I mention this to show the conditions with which these men are faced, and I say to you again that in relation to other classes of mechanics their basic rate of pay is no higher than those of bricklayers, plasterers, stonemasons, electricians and plumbers, and in many cases not so high. I make this statement because in my opinion the country should know that what has been said with regard to the trainmen is absolutely without foundation.
One other point I wish to deal with for a moment is the division of mileage. My hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario referred to it yesterday and indicated what certainly would take place. There is a misapprehension with regard to the division of mileage. I heard in the railway committee statements which were substantially exaggerated. Every man with a heart in his breast sympathizes with the men who are out of employment, but I know that the senior men who are being so much criticized have made very considerable voluntary reductions in the mileage they are taking. Let me refer for example to the shop men. They are entitled to work fifty-four hours a week and to receive pay for fifty-four hours, and voluntarily step by step they have reduced their hours, four hours now, four hours later on, and so on, until they are down to thirty hours a week, and they have done this in order to obviate the necessity of their fellow men being left without any work at all. And let me say that I am speaking in this regard with respect to lines which I know about. I cannot tell you what is taking place throughout the

country but I know of many terminals where the mileage rates have been brought down considerably, though not to as low a point as some would suggest as being necessary to afford employment to all. It is however a mistaken conception of what the men are doing to suggest that they are arbitrarily taking all that they can get, their pound of flesh, so to speak, and leaving all the other men out in the cold.
I will conclude as I started. I am supporting this bill, not because of anything I hope will result from it in its present form, but because I believe it is a step in the direction of showing the people of Canada what they are actually faced with, and proposing the only way by which they can get out of the difficulties they are in.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen opposite say, "hear, hear;" that may be their view. It is a subject for debate. It may be that in our day government ownership and operation is impossible. I do not believe it is. I believe that due control on the part of parliament, sympathetic control, would help to make government ownership and operation go very far. But so long as the government of the country owns a great national railway system, just so long must the ministry of the day take responsibility with respect to the essential features of that system. In my view that is the fundamental consideration; the ministry cannot possibly divest itself wholly of responsibility.
If the attitude is taken that the ministry should divest itself of all responsibility, what would it mean? It would mean that the ministry of the day is, to all intents and purposes, making a present to one man of the railway system of the country. He is to have entire control. It means you hand over the system to private control, because anyone who could do as he pleased with property would, to all intents and purposes, be in the same position as the owner of that property. We would be getting rid of government ownership and control if by legislation we said, "We will divest ourselves of all say and all control; we will not allow the people's representatives in parliament to have a word in regard to the matter, but we will give to one individual power to do as he pleases with respect to the whole system." That is the danger which I 53719-181
confess many hon. members on this side have seen in the legislation before us. It is a danger we wish to guard against. If by its provisions this bill really means that we are preparing the way for amalgamation, that such is the intention behind it, and further that we are freeing entirely both the executive and parliament from any control over this great national railway system, then we must be absolutely opposed to it. We would be opposed to that principle.
From the debate which has thus far taken place, the position of hon. members on this side of the house, has already been made fairly evident. We are all one with respect to doing everything we can to effect economies on the national railways. We are all one in regard to legislation which will further effective cooperation with the Canadian Pacific Railway, but which will maintain the integrity and identity of the Canadian National Railways as a government owned and controlled system. But we are unalterably opposed to an amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and we are unalterably opposed to divesting this parliament of its supreme rights in anything and in everything, and of taking away from this House of Commons its duty with respect to the control of expenditures of public moneys, which involve taxation.
There is the one further main division of the bill, namely that relating to the arbitral tribunal whose duty it is to settle disputes which may arise between the two companies, in the working out of a more effective cooperation. In connection with this part of the bill may I say I do not believe our views will be greatly different from those held by hon. members opposite, except as to the best form the tribunal can take. We recognize that there must be some tribunal to settle disputes, and that the establishment of the tribunal mentioned in the bill would probably serve a very useful purpose. Whether or not the tribunal suggested in the measure before us in the best one, is a matter open to debate. However, that may best be discussed when we reach the committee stage of the bill.
There are many who feel that, with its wide knowledge of railway matters, and the staff and equipment available to supply necessary information, the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners along with representatives of the companies could best act as an arbitral board. On the other hand there are some who do not hold that view. Again, this is a matter which can best be discussed in committee of the whole.
It seems to me that one real difficulty is tha t which presents itself where there is com-

pulsion with respect to something concerning which there may be a wish to bring about effective cooperation.
The principle involved is very much the same as that which has to be considered with respect to disputes generally. Some years ago this House of Commons debated at considerable length the merits of compulsory arbitration as against compulsory investigation in connection with disputes between employers and employees of the great public service utilities. The legislation of such countries as Australia which had compulsory arbitration laws upon their statutes was carefully studied in relation to the alternative of compulsory investigation leaving the enforcement of the award more or less to the force of an informed public opinion. At that time this parliament came to the conclusion that a compulsory investigation law which would bring out all the essential facts of the case, not to compel acceptance of the award but leave that to the operation of public opinion, would in the long run be more serviceable in the prevention and settlement of disputes than a system of compulsory arbitration. I think the decision made at that time was a wise one, and I believe its wisdom has been borne out by the experience of many years past in connection with industrial disputes. Take the railways, for instance. It is very seldom that one finds after a dispute has been carefully investigated by a board of investigation that the award made is not accepted by one side or the other. There is one aspect of the situation where it concerns railways which seems to me to make compulsory investigation the most effective method of dealing with matters of this kind. There is no party more concerned in the justice of a decision and the enforcement of a just decision than the community itself, and where a board of investigators is charged with full power to go into the merits of a case and disclose them publicly, I cannot conceive of many instances where public opinion would not be so strong as to compel the acceptance of a wise and just decision by both sides. My own personal feeling is that it would be advisable to take this step first, and try it out. We need not do everything at once; if it does not work, well and good. Something believed to be better can then be tried. W'e know that at least one of the companies is very strongly opposed to this compulsory arbitral feature, and it may be that it has strong reasons for feeling as it does. Where the parties can agree upon referring a dispute it may well be left to arbitration, the finding would then have to be

acceptable to both sides. But where one party is brought before a board in an unwilling frame of mind and feels that it is being coerced, that kind of thing cannot be kept up very long. I think, when we come to this phase of the matter, we ought to consider very carefully what it may be best to do.
I hope I am putting my position quite clearly. The house will appreciate that so far -as we on this side are concerned, we- are entirely at one with the government in the alleged objects of this bill, but I want to distinguish between principle and object. If there is any room for doubt as to the principle not being the same as the object, then we must be very careful with regard to the position we take. I want to accept the word of the minister that the principle underlying this measure is confined solely to the matter of cooperation, the effecting of economies and the improving of the system by freeing it from unnecessary and undue political control. On the other hand, I would not be true to myself, nor to hon. gentlemen on this side, -nor to the people of this country, if I did not point out that before we pass the second reading of this bill there should be no doubt whatever as to the principle which we are really supporting. With the view of removing any possible doubt in that regard, I have drafted an amendment in the nature of a privileged motion which I would like to move at this time. I move this amendment in the hope that it will be accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite, and that it may be the means of bringing hon. members of the house into a sufficiently united frame of mind to enable us to move on immediately to the committee stage, and there debate the possible differences between us. The minister said the other day that he hoped the house would not send this bill to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines or to the special committee on railways and shipping, but that it should be considered by the committee of the whole house. If that course is to be followed, there is an additional reason why at this time we should be absolutely certain of the principle we are supporting and which should govern and guide the committee in its discussions and deliberations. There should be some direction from the house to the committee of the whole as to the principles it wishes to have kept uppermost in the consideration of this measure.
The motion before the house is that the bill be now read a second time. I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for -Charlevoix-Sagai-enay (Mr. Casgrain):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be left out in order to insert the following instead thereof:	"the second

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
reading of this bill be postponed until this house have declared that nothing therein shall be taken to authorize any amalgamation of the Canadian National Railways with the Canadian Pacific company; or to divest parliament of its rights; or to take from the House of Commons its primary duty to control expenditures of public moneys and the taxes required to meet the same: and that the provisions of said bill shall be read in the light of this declaration, and be construed so as to conform therewith, and that in so far as any of its provisions may be inconsistent therewith they shall be amended accordingly,
and that the adoption of this amendment by this house shall constitute the declaration of its intention and purposes as set forth herein."
I should like to quote an authority which will help to explain the purpose I have in mind in moving this amendment. The citation from May under standing order 48, which is the order respecting privileged motions, reads,-I am reading from Beau-ehesnes Parliamentary Rules and Forms, paragraph 406:
The object of an amendment may be to effect suc-h an alteration in a question as will obtain the support of those W'ho, without such alteration, must either vote against it, or abstain from voting thereon, or to present to the house an alternative proposition either wholly or partially opposed to the original question.
In moving this amendment, I am not attempting to follow the second of the two courses mentioned in the rule; I am not presenting to the house an alternative proposition either wholly or partially opposed to the original question. What I am seeking to do is to effect such an alteration in the question as will obtain the support of those who, without such alteration, must either vote against it or abstain from voting thereon. I have not consulted with the members of the party generally, but I think I have a true impression of how they feel. I believe I can say for hon. gentlemen sitting on this side that if my right hon. friend will accept this amendment, all of us will be prepared to support the second reading of this bill. It will be thus made clear that our opposition, if opposition is necessary, is not to the principle of effecting economies, bringing about cooperation and helping to remove the national roads from political interference but to any enactment which would compel amalgamation of the national railway system and the Canadian Pacific or which would take away from this parliament or this House of Commons the rights which they should have at all times.
I hope I have followed the example suggested by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) in not attempting to make this a controversial discussion but to bring the political parties as close together as possible at this very critical time. I move this amend-53719-181J
ment in the sincere hope that it may be the means of enabling this House of Commons to take a united stand on this all important measure. May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment does not involve any lengthening of the debate or any delay in getting into committee. It will rather have the opposite effect; it will shorten discussion very materially. If the amendment is carried the house will declare as a guiding principle what the minister himself has declared already is intended, and also what I cannot conceive any government being willing to other than declare with respect to the right of parliament and the duty of the House of Commons. With the house expressing its opinion in this way, we shall feel a sense of security in supporting the principle of the bill for there will then be no possibility of mistake as to what we are supporting. But if that cannot be done, I must confess that so far as I personally am concerned I should not find it possible to support the second reading of this bill, because I would find in the refusal by the government of a declaration of this kind, evidence that there must be a sinister design which is not apparent on the face of the measure itself.
Mr. SPEAKER; Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the amendment?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to reserve the right to discuss the question whether or not the amendment is in order. In my judgment portions of it are not in order, but at the moment that is not a matter of importance.
The closing words of the right hon. gentleman opposite indicate clearly what was in his mind in the drafting of this amendment. When you speak of sinister motives or designs you can always be sure there is something of the kind behind a suggested amendment such as this. To suggest in a time like this that there are sinister motives in the introduction of the bill which is now before the house for second reading, and that these sinister motives are to be met by the introduction of the amendment just submitted is quite beyond me. However, the right hon. gentleman and his followers will have to adjust themselves to the necessary viewpoint to deal with that phase of the question.
I am going to make a very short review of the situation, Mr. Speaker, and of the legislation now before the house, and I think I can convince hon. members opposite that they are approaching this question from, shall I say, the wrong angle. The position is not, as has been suggested so frequently in this house, that these are the properties of the people of Canada. These are now the pro-

C.N.R.-C P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
perties of the people who loaned their money to build them, and under normal conditions they would take possession of them. It does seem to me that there are a few fundamental ideas which must be kept in mind in discussing these proposals. Let us look at them.
In Canada we had the Canadian Northern railway system, the Grand Trunk system, the Grand Trunk Pacific system, the National Transcontinental system and the Intercolonial line. These roads were the property of the crown with regard to the National Transcontinental and Intercolonial lines, and of private interests with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern. These properties were built with borrowed money, and that money was obtained largely through the guarantees given by the provinces and by the dominion which enabled the securities to be sold in the money markets of the world. In the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific the Grand Trunk gave its guarantee to the securities of the affiliated enterprise, it being the parent company. In the case of the Canadian Northern there were guarantees both by the provinces and by the dominion. Guarantees were given by a Liberal government in connection with the. construction of the line into Edmonton, and those who will look at the statutes of that time will find there an express condition that the road never should be amalgamated with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Guarantees were given by the province of British Columbia in regard to the construction of the old Canadian Northern from the mountains to the Pacific. We had the Canadian Northern Alberta, the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan and the Canadian Northern Ontario; we had various broken bits of line bearing the names of the provinces through which they passed, the securities of which were guaranteed by the provinces and by the dominion. The Grand Trunk railway system, which ran from Portland to Chicago, through Quebec and Ontario, combined a large number of branch lines and in fact, as is well known to those who are students of the railway question in this country, separate entities or companies still exist. For instance, there was the old Canada Atlantic, the line running from Ottawa to Parry Sound or beyond, the rails of which were carried to Coteau. These systems still exist; their securities are outstanding. They have been guaranteed in some instances by, we will say, the Grand Trunk; in others by other companies and in still others by the crown, but the fact is that the Grand Trunk system as such consisted of a large number of separate companies grouped together under one controlling management, and the very {Mr. Bennett.]
fact that they were bought at such a great cost had much to do with the subsequent financial difficulties of the Grand Trunk railway system.
It is needless for me to deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to-day. It was bankrupt before it was built; it was insolvent before it was completed. It passed into receivership and then came into the hands of the crown, really, under the amalgamation known as the Canadian National railway system. The Intercolonial railway was built by the people directly and owned by the crown. The millions of dollars that were invested in that enterprise were borrowed on the credit of the Canadian people plus a guarantee that was given, it will be recalled, under the provisions of the British North America Act, to enable the money to be obtained cheaply for its construction. That road was not located having regard to the best economic conditions; for strategic and other reasons it was built where it now is rather than where it should have been. These conditions were referred to during the course of this debate, but the money invested is the money of the people of Canada and not of any private enterprise. The obligation to repay the money was a direct obligation on the people of this dominion. The National Transcontinental, which represents an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars, was built in part from the surplus in the consolidated revenue fund, obtained from taxes imposed upon the people of Canada, and in part by borrowed money. It was to cost $13,000,000; it cost several hundred millions.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I shall not do more than indicate that these bankrupt enterprises were united into one system. When the decision of the privy council was finally given-and at that time the party of my right hon. friend was in power-an order in council was passed that brought all these systems under one control. They are known now as the Canadian National Railways. As I have said, they comprise the old systems to which I have alluded, together with the new roads built by the people of Canada-the National Transcontinental, the old Intercolonial railway, as well as the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk system, and the Canadian Northern.
The immediate effect of that amalgamation, not expressly stated in terms, has been to relieve the provinces of the weight of their guarantees, and if these guarantees were made effective against British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba those provinces would all be hopelessly bankrupt. That is

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
the railway position so far as the provinces in question are concerned.
Having been united under the conditions I have mentioned, they operated as an entity, as a system, and they carried on transportation from Portland to Chicago and in every province of Canada; and in the operating system was included the old Intercolonial railway. I wonder whether this house realizes just what the present position is. Sometimes I feel that the magnitude of the problem that confronts this parliament is little understood or appreciated. It is the greatest problem that confronts the Canadian people; it is the problem beyond all others that calls for the exercise of patience and in my judgment of much sacrifice on the part of the taxpayers. Why? Because not only have the provinces given their guarantees, but the dominion has given its guarantee with respect to the securities that are outstanding.
To what extent does the public own the securities of these systems that are now called the Canadian National Railways? Almost every hon. member knows, but I venture to repeat it. It amounts to nearly $1,300,000,000 -that is, nearly thirteen hundred millions of dollars are in the hands of the investing public in almost every country in the world, and securities representing the investment are guaranteed by the dominion or the provinces of this confederation.
Altogether?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am speaking of the
securities that are outstanding in the hands of the investing public of the world: Canada, the United States, Great Britain, continental Europe and even in the far east. Purposely, I do not mention the numbers of railway lines that have been brought into this system for prices that are little short of a public scandal; I do not mention that because it is unnecessary-it is past history so far as the act is concerned. As regards the branch lines, they have been built by the Canadian National Railways and by the Canadian Pacific Railway both, and in some instances duplication of facilities has brought disaster to both systems. I am not giving the exact figure; I said $1,300,000,000-it is $1,280,000,000 odd. That does not include the sums of money that have been paid out by the Canadian people from the consolidated revenue of Canada, or borrowed by them and handed over to these railways.
Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, just what that sum represents? It represents nearly one thousand millions of dollars. So that the two together, the securities that are now outstanding in the hands of the investing public,
representing roughly $1,300,000,000, plus the money that the Canadian people, either from surplus taxation or by direct loans made upon the sale of their own securities, have contributed, represent a total of nearly $2,300,000,000. And when I made the statement as to the investment by the crown, that is by the people, I did not include the interest upon the moneys thus invested. If I were to do so it might be almost unbelievable because the aggregate is so large.
Therefore we have this problem before us as Canadians: How can we so adjust conditions as to make possible the very lowest demand being made upon the Canadian taxpayer to provide interest to pay the annual requirements of the securities held by the public, to say nothing of the interest upon.^: the moneys which we have directly put into these enterprises? And that eliminates, of course, interest on the Intercolonial railway system.
Now we have another railway system in this country. That system was heavily subsidized by the Canadian people in land and money and it became a very great and prosperous organization. It is known in every part of the world. It was a competitor of the combined systems, now known as the Canadian National railway system. Sometimes, if I may be pardoned for saying it,
I wonder how intelligent men ever thought that it was possible to create three transcontinental systems of railways in Canada. Take the history of world transportation, take just the bald outlines of it, and ask yourselves how Canadians could ever have thought it possible to create a Grand Trunk Pacific transcontinental system, a Canadian Northern transcontinental system and a Canadian Pacific transcontinental system. It is beyond me. The other day I had brought to my attention a life of Sir Wilfrid Laurier written by a great friend of his, Senator David. In the 1905 edition, the first edition, the author opens one paragraph with the assertion that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not only a great orator but that he had clairvoyance inasmuch as he saw the future of the country when he brought forward the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. Later editions of the book leave that out. I need hardly point out that there must have been something in the minds of Canadians that now makes it impossible for us to understand who could have dreamed that three transcontinental railways could be sustained by eight million people.

They thought there would
be more.
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Of course they did; but
you could not project your mind into the future on any material that then existed that .vould warrant any such expectation, that you jould maintain three transcontinental systems .n this country.
If you have faith in your country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
One does not wish to
have faith in one's country to the extent of being foolish, and anyone knows that the mere suggestion that eight million or fifteen million people could sustain three transcontinental railway systems, over the territory these railways crossed, is absurd.
Now, I have been a witness to this. I saw these railways being built in western Canada. For thirty-five years I have lived there and I saw the development of transportation in that area. I remember the day the first Canadian Northern train reached Edmonton, and I remember when the Grand Trunk Pacific party came west for the purpose of considering the construction of their lines. I travelled west from Calgary to Banff with Mr. Hays and Mr. Morse and the prospective board of directors of that time, and I recall exactly what was then said. No one ever expected that there were going to be two systems then. People fully expected that the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific would be united into one system. Those who recall the dramatic moments in this house, though not in this particular chamber, when Mr. Blair left the government of that day, will remember as they recall it that he pointed out that what has happened would happen. It has happened even as he foresaw it. The point I desire to make is that we have received this as a legacy, and I think we have some right to ask hon. gentlemen opposite to give us their assistance in the solution of this difficulty. I say that for the reason that this party did not create it.
The people of Canada did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
