It created the trade
tangle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Under our constitution the measures that made possible the construction of those lines had to be initiated by the government of the day and they were initiated by the then governments of the day. This is not a question of the people of Canada; it is one of governmental action, the initiative being taken by the governments of the day for the eonstruction of those lines. But as I have said
fMr. Euler.]
frequently in public and made perfectly clear, I repeat in this chamber that the provinces of the west must assume an enormous responsibility with respect to the guarantees that they gave to the Canadian Northern system, without which guarantees that system would never have reached the coast. That is clear; every thoughtful man who examines the history of the matter knows that. In a period of universal depression, a period in world history the like of which has never been known before, this government has fallen heir to that condition. Having fallen heir to that condition, it had to seek as best it could some means for the solution of the difficulty that would not be wholly incompatible with the views of the Canadian people. I recognize the fact that no soft words are going to solve this problem, and no criticism of high taxation will pay the bills that result from it.
Let us see what has been done. Some hon. members may doubt the wisdom of the appointment of a royal commission; some may very properly say that the government of the day could have arrived at the same conclusions as those reached by the royal commission. But when you find the view put forward by the directing executive head of the national system and acquiesced in by the head of the Pacific system, that a royal commission was desirable in order that the problem might be studied from every angle, political considerations being eliminated, I think hon. members will agree that the government at least was warranted in taking the attitude it did. But I go further: this chamber approved that view. When the select committee made its report recommending that consideration be given to the views expressed by the railway executives, it will be recalled that the house acquiesced in that recommendation. There are those who say that the report of the royal commission does not advance the matter at all. In my judgment that commission gave more careful attention and consideration to the problem than is usually the case with public commissions. Let us for a moment examine it. The British interests, comprising practically 90 per cent of all the Canadian Pacific securities and the major part of the Canadian Northern securities that were issued prior to 1920, were represented by Lord Ashfield. My colleague, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), has pointed out to the house that in Lord Ashfield we had a man skilled in finance, an expert in the operation of transportation systems who, during one of his visits here, had to shorten it in order that he might return to deal with the complex problems arising out of the underground systems of transportation in the great city of

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
London. He came here, dispassionate, unprejudiced, and looked carefully over the situation. He traversed this country from ocean to ocean. The same may be said of his United States colleague. It is true that the latter was not a trunk line president. Owing to conditions that obtained in the United States at that time, the securing of the services of a trunk line president was absolutely impossible, but Mr. Loree is recognized by all railroad men in the republic to the south of us as having no superior so far as the practice and theory of railroading are concerned. He saw this problem with his own eyes. Then, if you take our own Canadians, I think most hon. members will agree that the chairman of the commission is a man whose position, and reputation as a jurist not only in this country but elsewhere, entitles us to have the utmost confidence in his dispassionate and judicial weighing of evidence and in the conclusions at which he would arrive. As regards the businessmen, Mr. Leman is the general manager of a bank but he has also had wide experience as an engineer. If my memory serves me aright, he is a graduate of McGill university and has wide experience. He concentrated his mind upon the problem. Certainly Sir Joseph Flavelle will, by the common consent of all who know him, be regarded as one of the foremost businessmen this country has yet produced. In regard to the selection of a gentleman from the extreme east I cannot do more than adopt what was said by my colleague the Minister of Railways, and everyone from western Canada who knows Professor Murray, president of Saskatchewan university, will agree that in considering this problem, he brought to it a skilled, disciplined mind, without prejudice. I think I am within the judgment of the house when I say that this commission considered the railway situation without fear, favour or bias. They examined the presidents of the roads, the directors, the financial comptrollers, the operating officials and they saw the roads themselves. They understood fully the duplication not only of trackage but of facilities. They saw all that was implied and involved in the branch line programs to which effect had been given and they learned with dismay of the financial position. They made a report. This government took the view that, the report having been received, the best way to proceed was to ask that a bill be prepared containing all the recommendations that had been made, that is for discussion only, and in the early stages it was thought it might be introduced into this chamber, but after consultation with my colleagues, it was concluded that a more ample opportunity for what one might call calm, dispassionate consideration of the problem, could be given if the bill were first introduced into the Senate.
I say this to my colleagues in the House of Commons, that I believe seldom has any committee given to a problem the same careful, thoughtful, unprejudiced consideration that was given to the bill by the Senate committee on railways. I am violating no confidence when I say that Lord Ashfield said to me in December last in England that he had read with the greatest interest the reports of that committee as they had been published and that he could not conceive of better consideration and attention being given to any matter than that evidenced by the work of that committee. The bill has been changed from *what it was originally; clauses have been added; clauses have been withdrawn, but in the main the principles continue to be those which the commission reported should be adopted. The government as such has in this legislation no object but one-to do what is best for the Canadian people. If constructive suggestions are offered from any corner of this house, the government will consider them on their merits, and they will be either accepted or rejected as they are considered sound or unsound. In other words, if the weight of argument would indicate that some view other than that indicated by the bill or some other clause should be adopted, the government is only too glad to avail itself of every assistance that may be offered. Why? Because the problem is not the problem of a government: it is the problem of the whole people, of this House of Commons and of parliament itself. In approaching that problem, let us see what the evidence discloses before I touch on the bill itself.
The evidence discloses not only the financial position to which I have alluded, but further that there is imposed annually upon the Canadian people a burden that amounts to many millions of dollars-roughly a minimum of one million dollars a week-to discharge the contractual obligations which the Canadian people, as taxpayers, have incurred. It is no good to say that we will repudiate those obligations. To do so is to destroy the credit of this country because the guarantees given constitute a contract to pay on the part of all the people of Canada just as though the securities were issued by the Canadian people without the medium of a railway at all. That is the difficulty of the position. Every year these moneys must be

C.N.R -C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
raised. Last year it is probable that some five millions of dollars may have been earned by the railways to take care of an obligation that amounted roughly, with capital expenditures, to between sixty-five and seventy million dollars. Does the true significance of that go home to the Canadian people, or even to this house? I looked the other day at the painting of Sir John Macdonald, and yet in the year that Sir John Macdonald died the entire revenues of the Dominion of Canada were not as great as the deficit of the Canadian National Railways we are now discussing, so rapidly has this country expanded and so limitless apparently have we thought our ability to provide the taxes, for in the end it becomes a matter of taxation.
Now what would happen under normal conditions if this were a private enterprise having defaulted in the payment of its obligations? What would happen would be that which took place in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific. An application would be made to the Exchequer court to appoint a receiver, the directors would pass out of existence, the receiver would take charge and would operate the system for the benefit of the bondholders or creditors of the road.
There has been introduced into this debate, as there was by others in another place, the thought that we are thinking of the financial interests as opposed to the human interests that may be concerned. Mr. Speaker, human interest centres in the employees of the system only if it continues to operate, for if it does not operate there is no employment, and unless a very, very great improvement is made in conditions the system as a whole cannot continue to operate. Every thoughtful man knows that. Everyone who has given attention to it knows that. Under normal conditions a receiver would be appointed by the courts. But there can be no receiver where you have the provinces and the dominion with their guarantees. The crown cannot default; the dominion and the provinces must pay or else their credit is done. Therefore, at the very threshold of the problem, the commission had to consider how to combine the powers of a receivership with the continued operation of a system that must if possible be maintained in operation, and so they selected three trustees. They did not call them trustee receivers, because the word would not be appropriate when dealing with the crown, because the crown does not go into a receivership. But nevertheless that was the condition with which they had to deal-default certain and positive for at least some period of time.

Under normal conditions the effect of a receivership, as every hon. gentleman knows, is that interest is no longer paid, and all the revenues are available to rehabilitate the system and bring about its reorganization. I am not going to take the time of the house this afternoon to mention more than one or two receiverships, but the great Milwaukee system went into receivership, as did Northern Pacific, the Union Pacific, the Santa Fe, the Wabash, and the Chicago and Great Western. All these roads went into the hands of receivers, and during the period of the receivership the security holders got no interest on their money. But you cannot do that in connection with our road because the provinces have given their guarantees and the dominion has given its guarantee as well. So we have the situation where this commission had to select a plan that would ensure the benefits of a receivership without in any sense restricting the operations of the system so far as that was possible from an economic standpoint. In other words, the legal necessities, together with all existing facts, made it essential that a body should be selected that would have all the powers of a receiver, together with the powers of a controlling management, to bring about that equilibrium between income and outlay that is the aim of every receiver before a reorganization takes place.
Why is the number three? It is the considered judgment of the commission, every one of them, that any number greater than three means disaster. That is their view. They do not put forward that view as politicians or as members of parliament. They put for-word that view as business men because they know that in the history of enterprises in which the effort to bring about an equilibrium between income and outlay has succeeded it has been necessary to have a small management. For the most part receiverships, which in the case of the railways I have mentioned were composed of two receivers, and if my memory serves me right, in one of the greatest the number was three. But the commission is very certain that any number greater than three will bring about a difficult if not an impossible situation.
I understand the difficulties involved-does any hon. member of this house think for a minute that living as long as I have in western Canada I do not understand the difficulty that anyone is going to have in explaining why you have only three trustees and they all living in one city, Montreal? Does anyone believe that I do not appreciate that difficulty, or that I seek it lightly and happily and

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
gladly? Of course not. But we accept it because we believe, on the balance of the arguments that are presented, that there is no answer to the fact that any number of men greater than three could not bring about what we are aiming to accomplish, the restoration of equilibrium between expenditures and income in the reorganization of the system. It is because we believe that any number greater than three means disaster, and that is based on experience that is universal.
I once heard Lord Buckmaster say that Lord Macnaghten, one of the greatest jurists of the Victorian era, said that the ideal number for a court of appeal was three, and he never changed his mind with respect to that. In England the highest courts, Divisions No. 1 and No. 2 are limited to three in number because experience has taught them that three is a much better number of men with which to deal with the problems than any greater number. I am bound to say that my own experience, which is not a matter of importance, and my observation, which is a matter of greater importance, and my reading, as well as the reasons presented to me, have convinced me beyond question that we should stick to the recommendation of three trustees in this matter. I put this to the house: Suppose we make the number five; those who have to deal with the matter or come after us will say, if success does not follow, "Why did you not follow the advice of the commission; why did you not accept their advice?" If one of the three is to be selected from one group or one class, then shall we say that political, racial, religious or occupational consideration shall prevail? Must it not be that these three men are selected with the same regard for merit, and for merit only, as induces a court to select a receiver?
The high court of parliament has now been called upon to determine how many men shall constitute the trustees for this system, to bring about again equilibrium between income and expenditures, and restore this road to a position where it will earn its way. The high court of parliament is now asked to accept or reject the advice which has been given by those who went out and studied this problem more carefully than you or I can study it-and their conclusion is that three is the number which should be appointed. I share that view. Apart from the arguments which their report indicates- and in my judgment they are conclusive- the experience of the world in dealing with matters of business is that when you have a situation, such as that to which I have alluded, there should be a small body of men constantly in consultation who will be able
to concentrate their minds upon the problem. And by that unity of effort which three, rather than five, can make possible, we will restore the property to the position in which we desire it. That is the fundamental recommendation with respect to administration. The directors disappear, not because the commission wanted to get rid of directors, per se; they disappear because of the financial position of this enterprise. They disappear because in a court of law, under normal conditions, they would thus disappear. And so it is that these trustees are substituted for the directors, by . the high court of parliament, just as the directors would be superseded in a court of justice, as was done in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific by a statutory receivership to preserve the property and to bring about, as I have stated, the equilibrium between income and expenditure.
I believe I have satisfied-at least, I trust I have satisfied the house, that the property is not the property of the people, except to the extent to which the people own the securities which are in default. INo interest has been paid upon it, and therefore it is fair to say that the Canadian people, as the holders of securities, have an interest in the enterprise. But this enterprise belongs to the investors; let us keep that in our minds.
How about guarantees?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am talking about
that-the people who have put their money into it and have not had any interest paid, and investors who have bought securities, have bought them on the strength of our guarantees. There is no question about that. Under those circumstances I trust this house realizes that many of the considerations which you and I, under normal conditions, would find operative in inducing us to arrive at a conclusion, must disappear. For we are now dealing'with very simple matters-securities, property in default, and security owners having a right to enforce their claims unless we, as guarantors, exercise our position and make payments. Under those circumstances I think-at least I hope-that the house will recognize just what the position is. Business men in this chamber, as they reflect upon the analogy between that and an ordinary joint stock company which is bankrupt, or as they reflect upon the history of great enterprises in this country, will realize how essential it was that the property be placed in charge of the numbers I have indicated for the purposes we and they have in view.
Some difficulty, apparently, has been experienced by hon. members opposite in the

C.N.R.-CJ".R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
thought that there is some sinister motive in this bill to bring about an amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I say to this house now that if that apprehension is grounded upon the fact that the section in the bill which was put in as it was originally drafted, has 'been taken out, is the cause of that apprehension, then we will restore it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Then we will restore it.
There is no thought of any trick to bring about something which we have pledged ourselves not to do. There is no sinister design behind this measure to accomplish the amalgamation of these systems, when this parliament is opposed to that being done. In my judgment it would be impossible to bring about the amalgamation of these two systems on any terms or conditions unless the people, themselves, had an opportunity so to declare. I have given much thought to the point as to whether or not the honest and proper method to pursue is, at the next general election, to afford an opportunity by plebiscite for the people to determine whether or not it is desirous that this should happen. It is true there was a plebiscite in this country concerning prohibition. It was not held at a general election, and the result gave us prohibition as they had it in England and free trade as they had it in Maine.
At any rate, let us leave that for the moment. I desire to make it abundantly clear to the house that in my judgment no government could ever have any mandate which could be regarded as ample to warrant it in taking the step to which reference has been made, unless it proceeded from the direct authority given by the people who owned the equity of redemption. The people of this country own not the road but the equity of redemption. And so long as the government of Canada is Father Christmas and pays under the guarantee, just so long, there being no foreclosure, that equity of redemption has a right to express its views as to what shall be done. And it can only in my judgment be done in the manner I have indicated, by affording to every citizen who, in the end, owns the equity of redemption, an opportunity to express an opinion for or against amalgamation.
In order that there might be no misapprehension, in order that hon. members might be deprived of an opportunity of casting even a suspicion of bad faith upon the government-although I do hesitate to deprive hon. members opposite of an argument-at any rate in order that they might be deprived of that argument, I desire to say we will

place in the bill in adequate terms words which will make it clear that there may be no amalgamation of the two systems nor destruction of their integrity under and by virtue of this measure. And I may say that when I first heard of it my colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) had not learned that such a suggestion was in the mind of anybody, because I do not believe this bill is susceptible of any such construction being placed upon it.
But it could possibly be interpreted in that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I hardly think it is fair
to say that there is any such possibility. But lest there be, I desire to remove that stumbling block from the cooperation which the right hon. gentleman desires. We will make that clear.
Now, let us proceed one step further, the desire to eliminate politics from the control and operation of the system. I am not going to dwell upon that phase of the matter. I am not even going to digress at length, beyond saying that the commissioners thought it was wise, not as an insult to members of parliament or the Senate, but as a principle which they thought should be made effective, that members of this parliament, whether in the Senate or the House of Commons, should not be eligible for appointment as trustees. They had no desire to insult any member of this parliament, whether in one house or the other, but they desired to make it abundantly clear that the whole principle was that the benefits which accrue from privately owned operation should be made available for this road. That is why they put that provision in the bill. It was struck out in the Senate because hon. gentlemen thought that there was some reflection upon their fitness. I do not so construe it and I hope it will be the will of this house to restore such a provision in order that there may be no question of that kind with respect to the measure.
Leaving aside the question of politics, leaving aside the necessity of this action being taken, we come to the methods suggested in the measure to accomplish the ends desired. As I have indicated there is, first, cooperation by agreement and, second, cooperation by direction where the parties fail to agree. If there is no amalgamation and if the object which must be always kept in mind when a property is placed under trustees or receivers is to be attained, it must be done in one of two ways. It must be done either by amalgamation with its competitor or cooperation with its competitor so as to eliminate waste-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
t'ul and useless services. I warn every hon. member of this house, including myself, that we must be prepared to put up with great sacrifices to attain our end. It is no good for a member to come into this house and say:
I have only a train once a week on my branch line, I should have six trains a week. It is no use to say: I must have three trains a day instead of one. It is no use to carry on political agitation and intrigue for the purpose of enforcing that upon the government. Just so long as you have a government able to control the management, just so long will you have intrigue and combinations to force upon the management the views of the government and its supporters. These are times for plain speaking, and there is no hon. member now looking me in the face who does not know that rvhat I say is true. I know it is as as true as the fact that I am looking at hon. gentlemen opposite.
Let us face the facts. Let us realize that the reason cooperation is provided for in this bill in the terms it is is to make effective the purposes of the bill. How else are we going to do it? I will admit it is drastic but modern surgery says that if you will cure, the operation must be radical where the evil is deep-seated. This is a surgical operation and it must be a radical operation. In order to make it effective and successful we must eliminate every political consideration which would interfere with the success of the operation. This is not a pleasant thing to say. There are hon. members in this house within sound of my voice who the moment I said what I have said began to think in terms of what it was going to mean in votes in a particular locality. We are all human, but we must not forget that we have a larger obligation. Our effort must be to save not the road alone but, as I said, because of the guarantees that have been given, the credit of the guarantors themselves.
Let us go a step further and deal with cooperation by agreement. The minister gave evidence of what might be accomplished when one had the purpose and the intention to accomplish. There is no doubt that all one has to do is to take the time tables and he will see where cooperation by agreement will accomplish a great deal of saving, bring about many economies and prevent waste.
We come now to the second point with reference, to which I should like to make a few observations, cooperation by direction as the result of arbitration. Some hon. members of this house regard this measure as one that interferes with the statutory and corporate rights of the Canadian Pacific Railway. My
examination of the facts so far as I have been able to look behind the scenes leads me to conclude that that clause was put in by those who -were responsible for it because they thought it would be beneficial to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. There is no one who would interfere with the corporate powers granted to that road just merely for the sake of interfering. When the railway commission came into being it was clothed with powers which gave it the right to interfere here, there and elsewhere. It is true' that it may be said that this provision came about by reason of agreement but leaving all aside for the moment, it must be remembered that we have always claimed the right, either by the governor in council before the railway commission or by the railway commission exercising its statutory powers, to deal with problems affecting the rights of the people with respect to the railroads that serve them. The theory is that all corporations created by this parliament are created for the purpose of serving the people and the basis of this statutory cooperation-that is what we will call it-is that it must be beneficial. There can be no arbitration under this bill unless the cooperation sought by arbitration is cooperation that will result in good to the systems affected. It must be beneficial to both systems, not only to one. The condition precedent to the exercise of the compulsory powers of arbitration, a condition which must be determined antecedently to the powers being exercised, is that as a result of the exercise of these powers, if they are exercised, benefits will result to both systems. That is the basic principle of the statute, that benefits must result to both before the arbitral powers can be exercised.
I shall not transgress too long upon the time of the house, but I want to say one word more with respect to the control of parliament. If I have not been unfair, and I do not think I have, in stating the general purposes and intentions of the measure, the house will agree with me that we must eliminate the possibilities of what I shall call interference with this extraordinary management. Even as receivers or trustees have to go to a competent court to receive their powers, their authority and their right to issue securities if the earnings are not sufficient, just so is this parliament the high court to which these trustees must always come. There is no other court to which they can go for the purpose of discharging their duties under this statute. The statute renders them independent as though they were the operators of a private system but it renders them subject to all the control
2S62

C.N.R.-C.P.R. BUI-Mr. Bennett
to which a private system would be subject. Further, it does more; it provides-I think the right hon. gentleman must have overlooked this-that this parliament must supply the money for the deficits.
We did not overlook that.
And have no control otherwise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If that is so, what further control can be had in anything except the control to grant or withhold supply?
After the money is spent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not at all; a budget has to be presented. If the hon. gentleman has not read the act I may tell him that it provides that a budget must be presented, and this parliament gives its sanction and approval in order that it may have that power and control that is essential. I put this to the house, Mr. Speaker: How would it be possible for these trustees to function and operate if they were to be subject to the governor in council? I put that problem to the house and to every individual member. What is the governor in council? The governor in council is the government of the day.
Responsible government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have heard it otherwise described in this house by hon. gentlemen opposite. I suppose government by order in council, which rescinded a contract for $4,000,000 for a hotel in Vancouver, substituting contracts that brought the cost to $11,000,000, is responsible government. That may be responsible government, but responsible to whom? The problem which this house and this country faces is not to be glossed over by any talk about constitutional rights or parliamentary powers such as this. Can parliament create a body with such powers as would be exercised by a private enterprise and still have control by reason of having to find the necessary money to enable them to function? I say yes. That is what is embodied in this statute. That is parliamentary control in its broadest and best sense; that is responsible government. Not a dollar can be found for this road or for these trustees; no money can be advanced to enable them to meet the obligations that have been imposed upon the roads by the guarantees alike of provinces and the dominion, unless this parliament grants it to them. That is the essential control that parliament must exercise, and if I so desired I could name many commissions both in England and in Canada in which we find the same situation.

I desire to avail myself of this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to say that if government ownership is to succeed it can only do so if it observes the same business maxims that are observed by private enterprises. It cannot succeed if those who administer it are to be dragooned on the one hand by their political friends and attacked on the other hand by their political foes. It cannot succeed if its policies are made the football of contending parties. It can only succeed if it has the same free, untrammelled opportunity under the laws of the country that is afforded private enterprise. The corporate position of these trustees must be the same as the corporate position of the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Both are under the law; both control properties; both exercise their powers to the best of their ability, with an eye singly directed to the success of the enterprise. If this parliament should be dissatisfied with their conduct action can be taken any year when it is asked to provide means and money for the operation of the system. No one will complain, I am sure, if the time ever comes when they do not have to apply to parliament for money, but if parliament in its wisdom, in the exercise of its plenary powers, is dissatisfied, it can declare that it will not give them further money unless they vacate their offices. Parliament has complete control. Anyone who knows the fundamentals of government knows this is so. This house, in its power to vote money, has complete control over that board of trustees, and parliamentary control can never be more strongly exercised than it can under these very powers.
I shall not deal longer with this phase of the matter, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to say that when subsection 6 of section 9 is referred to it must be perfectly clear that the crown is the crown as a shareholder, because as a shareholder the crown owns the Canadian National system. The words "any other shareholder" of course contemplates to the crown as a shareholder. With respect to the possibility of amalgamation being brought about by an indirect method when it could not be directly accomplished, the section that we will offer will provide against both direct and indirect means, so the house need have no fear in that respect.
Now I should like to say a word or two with respect to the amendment. I hope the right hon. gentleman will withdraw it. Perhaps my hopes are beyond my expectations, but for a moment let us look at what it contains. It asks that the second reading of this bill be postponed, and of course that means the end of the bill.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
No, it does not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hold on a moment. Look at the rules with respect to the six months hoist and the three months hoist. The postponement of the second reading of this measure means an interference with its orderly passing in this house under the government of the day.

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I submit that under the ruies of the house this amendment can be put and, if it is carried, the house can immediately proceed with the second reading of the bill.
I do not think that is a point of order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: I should like to ask my right hon. friend this question: If this measure were passed to-day could parliament remove the chief trustee to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
In what way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
May I interrupt the Prime Minister for a moment. I should like to direct his attention to section 7 of the bill which provides:
No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Surely.
I would ask my right hon. friend whether that does not make this House of Commons subject to the will of the Senate with respect to the salary to be paid to the chief trustee named therein.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But it is the same with respect to the judges. This followed the provision with respect to the judges, that is all; it desired to place the trustees beyond the influence of political control and to give them the same position of independence as the judges enjoy. They can be removed only by a joint address of the Senate and the House

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bennett
of Commons. Let me go further however. If this parliament, notwithstanding that provision, saw fit to pass a statute the day after tomorrow repealing that section, it has the power to do so. Everyone knows that.
The Senate would have to be in agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, of course; you cannot pass any bill unless it is passed by the commons, the Senate and the crown, for those three constitute parliament; there is no parliament without that conjunction. Let me quote further:
And that the provisions of said bill shall be read in the light of this declaration.
Well, all bills are read in the light of that declaration; there is no bill on the statute books that is not read in the light of that declaration. But, I ask, why should we adopt, as a preliminary of the second reading of the bill, a short essay on responsible government? I ask that question without offence. All bills, I say, are passed in this country in the light of that declaration, and to suggest that this bill should be singled out as one that shall be passed in the light of that declaration is to put it mildly to do violence to constitutional practice and authority. Further:
And be construed so as to conform therewith, and that in so far as any of its provisions may be inconsistent therewith they shall be amended accordingly.
In other words, before you know what is to be done, Mr. Speaker, you are asked to adopt amendments in this house. The time for this of course is when the bill is in committee, the time for it is when amendments are under consideration in the committee; the time is when an opportunity may be offered for consideration and discussion, when we know whait we are dealing with. But as regards this pious declaration that the rights of parliament are not to be taken away in the passing of this bill, and that the control of public expenditures is in the hands of the House of Commons-that is only partly true, unfortunately; they are in the hands of parliament, for the Senate sometimes rejects money bills. I wonder if it is beyond the memory of hon. members that the Senate rejected the Yukon bill by which a subsidy was provided for the construction of that road; I wonder if it is beyond the memory of the house that the Senate rejected a bill in the days of Sir John Macdonald with respect to a section of the Canadian Pacific that passes through the State of Maine. Is that beyond the memory of hon. gentlemen? The statement should be that parliament controls, for no bill that

is passed by this house, not the budget bill, becomes law until it is passed by the second chamber and assented to by the crown. There are three divisions of government in this country-the legislative and executive and of course the judicial, which we leave out for the moment; and the legislative divides itself into three branches: the commons, the Senate and the crown. Now, this is a suggestion that only the commons shall be concerned in the matter before us. Let me point out however that we cannot adopt any such statement as the law of the country, not even to oblige my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth)-that the commons is the only house. There is still a reformed Senate.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen laugh, but I read in a newspaper that it had been reformed by death-that was some years ago. So that it is hardly fitting that we should endeavour to insult one house of parliament by adopting a resolution to the effect that the control of expenditures of public moneys, and the taxes required to meet the same, shall not be taken away from the House of Commons.
"Primary duty" are the words used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, to take from the
House of Commons its primary duty.
That is what it says.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But that is not its primary duty.
It is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Its primary duty?
Certainly it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That shows you, Mr. Speaker, how difficult it would be to adopt this essay as a preamble to the bill before us, because there are differences of opinion as to whether or not that is so. The primary duty of the House of Commons is not the control of expenditures of public moneys and of taxes.

What else is
it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The primary duty of the House of Commons, as the right hon. gentleman knows, is to legislate. That is its primary duty; that is its job. And what is more, no legislation enacted by this House of Com-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Ilsley
mons with respect to public expenditures or taxes is law until the other two branches of our system of government have functioned, namely, the Senate and the crown.
The right hon. gentleman knows that under the constitution of the mother country and of this country the right of the House of Commons over taxation and expenditures is fundamental.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not what this
amendment says. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Mackenzie) and myself will not be in disagreement as to fundamentals; the only difficulty is when you speak of the primary duty of the House'of Commons. The fundamental duty of the House of Commons is, as between it and the Senate, to control expenditure of money; but the Senate has gone on record as saying that in this country that is not so. You will find that in the sessional papers of the Senate. They have the power to amend any money bill.
Does the right hon. gentleman believe in that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not the point I
am discussing at the moment. The hon. gentleman's question reminds me of the stock question always put to the youthful candidate, "When will the hon. gentleman stop beating his wife?" I do not propose to answer that question. If it will be of any interest to the hon. gentleman. I may say to him frankly that I have always thought that so far as the control of expenditures is concerned the Senate had the power only to accept or to reject but not to amend. That has been my personal view.
I think I have covered the situation, and while I suppose it is not to be hoped for, I suggest that this amendment should be withdrawn. We propose to proceed with the bill and we ask the united assistance of the house in giving it the second reading and affording to every member of the house, on our own as well as on the opposite side, an opportunity to make any suggestions that may be at variance with the provisions of the bill as they now read.
It is my earnest hope and sincere desire that, realizing that the government of the day merely happens under our constitution to be the' spokesman as between, the crown on the one hand, who must initiate, by message, any legislation involving money, and the house on the other, hon. members will adopt the bill after the fullest possible opportunity has been afforded for considering any amendments that mas' be suggested by the other side; and
we will assume the responsibility for incorporating in the measure a provision that nothing therein contained shall be taken, read or construed as authorizing directly or indirectly any amalgamation of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific systems.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), in the course of his speech this afternoon, made one statement with which I agree, and that is that the government has some right to the assistance of hon. gentlemen on this side of the house in dealing with this very important railway problem. Having listened to many of the speeches that have been made in this debate and having read the ones which I did not hear, I believe they have been of such character and quality that they must have been of considerable assistance to the government in its effort to deal with this problem. That applies to the speeches not only from the other side, but from this as well. There are many respects in which most of us on this side are in agreement with the Prime Minister. Many of the statements which he made this afternoon will not meet with much disapproval from opposition members. But there are some respects in which most of us, at least on this side of the house, cannot agree with him, and I shall deal with those before I finish my remarks. [DOT]
In a general way this railway problem which confronts the Canadian people admits of three possible solutions. The first is the continuation of. the system which at present exists, that is of more or less unrestricted competition between the two great railway systems. There are some advocates of that course, some persons who believe we can safely leave the solution of this problem to the systems themselves. They point to the great economies which have been effected recently by the voluntary efforts of the executives of the two systems, and they consider, by a continuation of those efforts in the direction of economy, the Canadian Pacific can be put upon a dividend paying basis and the Canadian National Railways can be put upon an interest paying basis. I am, however, afraid that that view is based upon too optimistic an expectation. I fear that the return of prosperity will be so long deferred that if the country does not take some more drastic steps than a policy of laissez-faire,

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. llsley
within a year or two it will be driven to take very drastic steps. So I do not agree with a policy of continuation of unrestricted competition between the two systems.
The second proposal, one which, I think, is propounded by some hon. members but not very many, is the one which we have come to call amalgamation. By amalgamation I do not mean the sale or transfer of the Canadian National property to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That is advocated by very few people. I mean unified management of the two systems. When we are speaking about amalgamation as a practical proposition, we mean unified management by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company of all the railways in the Dominion of Canada. There are those who believe unified management under government ownership would be advantageous, but it may be dismissed from one's mind as being beyond the realm of the practical, because there is such a large volume of outstanding liabilities of the Canadian Pacific-and I mean' by that their share capital as well as their bonded indebtedness -that no practical proposal has been placed before the Canadian people whereby provision can be made for a return of the investment of those who have put their money into the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. So when we are speaking of amalgamation, we mean amalgamation under the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I do not propose to argue at any great length for or against amalgamation, because to all intents and purposes it is not a < live issue in this house. One has only to listen to this debate and to hear hon. members on both sides express their convictions, to realize that public sentiment is such that the Canadian people at the present time would not approve amalgamation of the two railway systems. There are many reasons for that, the strongest of which is, I suppose, that it is feared that to give the operation of 40,000 miles of railway to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would be to place too much power in the hands of one great corporation, and just as the radio committee last year, finally, by unanimous vote, rejected the proposal of Mr. Beatty that the channels of radio communication in this country be all handed over to a great private corporation, so the house and the Canadian people generally would at this time undoubtedly by a large vote reject any proposal that our channels of transportation be handed over to a great private corporation. Therefore I do not think I need spend much time in discussing amalgamation. It is quite possible that greater economies would be

effected by amalgamation than by any other proposal we could adopt. Mr. Beatty's estimate of the economies that could be effected is, I think, $75,000,000. That may or may not be too large an amount. They can be brought about only by the scrapping of whole communities, the taking up of thousands of miles of rails and the displacement of an enormous number of labourers, and at present at least, serious as the situation is, the solution known as amalgamation is for all practical purposes out of the question. The benefits it would bring would be purchased at too great a price.
That brings us to the third proposal, the only other one that has been placed before the Canadian people, and that is the proposal * along the lines of the recommendations of the Duff commission. It may be summed up in this: competition with cooperation, with provisions for enforcing the adoption of cooperative measures where the two systems themselves are not able to agree upon them. With that principle I am in accord. I arrive at that conclusion by the process of elimination. It seems to me to be the best of the three proposals. It has, of course, many difficulties. The very term "compulsory cooperation," which so many persons apply to that proposal, involves in one sense a contradiction in terms. But in many walks of our business and industrial life there is cooperation together with competition, and while the experiment is a very difficult one to perform successfully, still I would be prepared to support the main principles underlying part III of Bill A of the Senate which is now before the house for consideration.
Let me come now to the bill itself. To begin with, I do not agree with the Prime Minister when he would have the house adopt the view that because great care was taken in bringing together experts in the Duff commission and because those men have met with great success in their various walks of life, the bouse should adopt their proposals without modifications. Nor am I greatly impressed either by the very able committee of the other house of this parliament. In this House of Commons we must exercise as honestly and as fearlessly as we can our own intelligence. AVe are very likely to be impressed by the opinions of successful men, but often men who have made a great success of their own business do not' know what is best for a government or a parliament or a legislature to do. One can look around and see instance after instance where these successful men have made most horrible mistakes in the legislative sphere because the principles which have made them successful

Mr. Speaker, in discussing this extremely important measure in which is embodied many months of labour and arduous research upon the part of a royal commission and many weeks of careful consideration upon the part of the Senate and its committee, I must keep in mind, and we should all keep in mind, that under the rules of this house there are two distinct aspects under which it can be considered. While these two aspects are inseparable and interrelated, while they form two parts of the one whole, each must be discussed at its own time and upon the appropriate occasion. I intend to confine my remarks wholly to the underlying principles of this measure, leaving the discussion and consideration of the methods by which these principles shall be carried out until we are in committee of the whole.
As I see it, and I believe this is the feeling commonly held throughout the house, there are three main principles embodied in this measure. First, there is the principle, implied rather than expressed but discussed and agreed to on every side of the house, of maintaining the integrity of the two systems as separate entities. It may rightly be said, as it has been said, that this is a somewhat academic subject at the moment, that the time may come when it will become a matter of real consideration, so on that aspect I shall say only this: If and when the time does come that in the opinion of the people of this country and the parliament of Canada we should, for the well being of Canada, have one great rail-fMr. Ilsley.]
road monopoly, I do not believe the people will tolerate anything other than a state monopoly. It is quite obvious, and it has been stated again and again, that there is a great difference in principle and in effect between a monopoly in the hands of the people and controlled by the state and a monopoly in the hands of a private body of citizens no matter how eminent or how desirous of doing right that body may be. Transportation is not only a business in itself, it makes possible all other business and all other enterprise. To create a private monopoly in transportation would be to create something in the nature of a giant octopus which would have the power, even though it might lack the will or intent, to strangle any industry or any community in any part of Canada. On the other hand, if a state monopoly became inevitable, it would be held by a body which represented every industry and every part of Canada and to which all of Canada could look with confidence for fair dealing and fair play. At this time I merely indicate as my own unalterable conviction, and what I believe to be the unalterable conviction of every man and woman in this country who has thought about the subject, that if the time does come that there should be an amalgamation of the two great transportation systems, that amalgamation must be a publicly owned monopoly operated by the state.
I come now to the next main principle, efficient management. Here again I find myself in accord with the measure now before us. This is a question of the transfer of management and operating responsibility from a large directorate exercising very small powers and having very vague and dubious authority, coupled with a president who exercises practically entire authority, financial as well as operative, to a small body of trustees, which would not only exercise the authority now vested in the directorate but have the financial control now exercised by the president. I did not intend at the moment to discuss the number of trustees that should be appointed. In spite of what was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in what I looked upon as a very able address, in spite of the pronouncement of the royal commission which examined into the facts, and in spite of the view of the Senate which examined into the evidence and drew their own conclusions, I am not at all certain that a somewhat larger body of trustees, possibly representative in character, would not be better and would not be more effective.
What is the underlying motive of this measure? What was it that made necessary the appointment of the commission, and what

interests should we have in mind in dealing with the situation? It is vital to them, in respect of freight and passenger rates, that these shall be reasonable and shall bear a fair relation to the value of the goods or commodities transported, or, in respect of service, that it shall be adequate and shall provide that which is necessary for the carrying on
of their business, whether in buying or in selling. Strange though it may be these two interests, conflicting at times, are still the interests of the same people and must be considered by this house when dealing with the matter. It would be just as fatal were we to sacrifice the interests of the people in respect of freight and passenger rates and transportation service upon the altar of finance as it would be were we to forget the financial side, the tremendous burden of liabilities and the plight of the taxpayer, and consider only the needs of this country by way of transportation service. Then, too, for we are all interested in this question from various angles, we cannot forget the labour problem which is involved and which has been placed before this house so ably by different hon. members, particularly those who directly represent labour. We cannot forget the service they have rendered; we cannot forget their future, their families, their lives and their prosperity. So 1 say, Mr. Speaker, that in examining this problem we must consider the various aspects from which it must be approached. Of that, however, I may have a w'ord to sa}' later. At any rate there is the second of the principles involved, the efficiency of management, and let me repeat that. I believe in the principle of a relatively small body of trustees, devoting their whole time to the task and given as their responsibility the job not only of outlining the general policies and supervising the operations of the Canadian National Railways but of assuming responsibility for the financial policies of the system, the lack of which has been partly responsible for our present plight.

As to the question of the number of members of the board of trustees and the mode of appointment I shall have more to say. However, I consider this to be a matter of detail which can be well left to the time when the house is in committee, when it can be discussed with greater knowledge and greater result. In passing I will merely suggest not only that possibly a somewhat larger body of trustees might be more efficient and more representative, having in mind the various aspects to which I have already alluded, other than those financial, but that some consideration might be given the mode of appointment and particularly of reappointment, which has been said by the hon. member who immediately preceded me (Mr. Ilsley) to make the board of trustees at least partly a self-perpetuating body. I think when we reach committee of the whole some thought might be given that aspect of the question, and perhaps some definite changes might be made.
We come now to the third principle, and there again, speaking as a matter of principle only, I think there is hardly a member of the house who is not in full accord with the principle of reasonable cooperation between those two great systems. Again I am speaking of the principle of cooperation, not necessarily of the details of the machinery by means of which we seek to bring it about. This has been spoken of as a system of compulsory cooperation, and perhaps to some slight degree it might be so termed, though I should hardly call it such myself. It begins, of course, with the opportunity for and the suggestion of voluntary cooperation, the same principle which has been carried into effect during recent months, and the suggestion is that it be carried as much further as circumstances may reasonably permit. Then what? This legislation does not seek to give to any committee or to any appointed body the power to suggest and initiate cooperative policies. It really proposes to appoint a committee of arbitration, who shall deal with proposals which will be brought forward by one or other of the lines, or by both acting together, upon the details of which they fail to agree. If it were compulsory in the true sense of the word the legislation would give to that committee the power of initiating and suggesting methods of cooperation. This is rather a measure of compulsory arbitration on matters brought to the notice of the appointed board of arbitration by the railway systems themselves. I think the principle there embodied is perfectly sound. However, we must remember to differentiate very clearly and definitely between the principle and the method by which that principle

is brought into effect. After all, as is the case in so many matters both public and private, the essential and vital thing is the spirit and the ability of the men who exercise those powers and who seek to put the act itself into full operation. The success of this movement, the success of any effort towards cooperation through the medium of this board of arbitration, will depend wholly not only on the mentality of the men who compose that board, but upon the spirit with which they approach their task, in which spirit may be reflected fairly closely the underlying motive and the real purpose which lies behind this measure and the entire investigation.
It will I think be recognized quite frankly and readily that all cooperation through which economies are effected must mean the reduction or the elimination of certain services. Where for example two lines are found where only one is required, and where in consequence operating costs rise far beyond the point they otherwise would reach, it is obvious that the only economy that could be brought about through cooperation would be by the abandonment or closing-down of one of these two lines. This is a case in which the arbitration board will come into play. Now we will take it that one of these lines must of necessity be a privately-owned line belonging to the Canadian Pacific and the other must be a Canadian National line belonging to or controlled by the people, and it is of the utmost importance, it is vital to the purpose of this measure, vital to the realization of our hopes and expectations, that these men shall approach their task certainly with an impartial mind, for the opportunities would be vast and numerous to throw the weight of influence and the benefit of the cooperation one way or another. We have therefore to ask this question and frankly face it: Is this economy to be for the benefit and in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer, or is it to be in the interests of vested capital? There is a matter that cannot be ignored, a matter that can be fully understood only when this measure is in operation. I am hoping that when it is in full operation at least fair play will be given both. But if there is to be a question one way or the other, if we have to balance and weigh one against the other, if we must help one to the detriment of the other, then I hope that it will be the Canadian people as a whole, the taxpayers of the country, who will receive the benefit of any doubt that may exist.

I speak of the invested capital as found in the privately-owned system, not as found in *the publicly-owned system, because the bondholders of the publicly-owned system-and I still use that word owned for reasons to which I shall allude-the bondholders of the Canadian National Railways, I say, are in a preferred position in this time of depression. Theirs is not the responsibility; theirs is not the risk. In their case the interests of vested capital and the interests of the taxpayer become one and the same thing, because the taxpayer must stand behind the system, guaranteeing the returns of the vested capital itself. On the other hand however we have vested capital owned by bondholders and stockholders, and while I believe in treating them fairly may I reiterate that in the spirit of the measure, in the spirit of its enforcement, in the spirit of the arbitration which may come to pass from time to time I hope that the larger object will be kept in view and that the interests of the people as a whole will be the predominating and prevailing influence.
One or two matters have come up to which I would refer for a moment. There is for example the statement of the Prime Minister, at least the inference he drew, that the real owners of the Canadian National system, notwithstanding the opinion often expressed in different parts of this house, are not the Canadian people but the bondholders who have invested their money in those lines now forming the Canadian National railways, and the payment of whose interest on capital was guaranteed by the people of the country. I must confess that I find myself somewhat under a handicap in differing from the Prime Minister. Not only is he a man of great ability and wide experience but he is a lawyer of high repute, w'hile I am a layman lacking his experience and, I am free to confess, his ability. But at the same time I cannot understand the position as he takes it. In the first place, and following his own argument, w'hat do we find? We find that the bondholders have certain rights, certain vested interests in these lines. They do not own them; they are not shareholders; they have loaned money to them and have taken a mortgage, and until such time as they foreclose and throw the lines into the hands of a receivership, surely the people of this country who are now the shareholders must own the property. And until the people of this country default in their payment of interest, until they fail in their obligations, until they give notice that no longer will they be responsible, until then surely there can be no question as
to who, actually speaking, are the owners of the property. When that time comes it will be a question indeed as to who may own the railways thereafter, after the receivership may have been called for; for, again, I cannot agree that the appointment of this board of trustees is in effect the appointment of a receivership to take over a ruined and bankrupt undertaking and if possible to set it on its feet, administering it in the meantime in the interests of those financially concerned. I cannot look on it in that light, because after all it is an undertaking vital to the wellbeing of Canada; it is an undertaking vital to the people not only from the point of view of finance but also from the point of view of service; it is an undertaking which under no circumstances will the people of Canada allow to stop or fail. We know that.
Now we are going to put these men in control for one purpose and one purpose only, namely, to serve the interests of the true owners of the railways, and that is the Canadian people from Halifax to Vancouver. That brings me to the point raised by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and to which exception has been taken by some others, and that is, the attributes, the point of view, the mentality which we should look for in our trustees. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), I think it was, rather objected to the idea that we should expect these trustees to be believers in the principle of public ownership, and he suggested that this was no part of their qualifications into which we should inquire. Were he speaking of the railway commission, whose functions are judicial, whose duty it is to act impartially as between public ownership on the one hand and private ownership on the other, I should be inclined to agree with him. Were he speaking of the arbitration committee which will be set up and whose duties, again, are impartial and cooperative, I might say yes. But when he is speaking of a body of trustees whose duty and responsibility it is to manage for the people of Canada a property entrusted to their care, then I take issue with him. For who are their employers? The people, all the people, and their interests must be served. But how can their interests be well served by men who do not even believe in the principle under which they are employed? How can the interests of a railway still in competition with a private road be properly served by a body of trustees who disbelieve in the principle under which the lines they control are managed and run, and who in their hearts incline towards the principles of the competitive

Another important point has been raised, upon which there is some difference of opinion, and which becomes of even greater importance as we go further into the question. This is the matter of political interference. It has become habitual in the house and, indeed, throughout the country, to look with shuddering horror upon the slightest approach to political influence or interference in matters of business. The conviction is apparently held not only in the country, but in the house, that the moment a politician lays his blighting hand upon any enterprise, it is damned and doomed to failure. If that be true, it is a tremendous indictment not only of the individual members of the house, but of the very system which sends them here. If it oe true, it means that the fact that members are elected to this house of parliament, the fact that they belong to institutions such as this, so unfits them foir any other task that any business matter they approach will be managed inefficiently and is bound to fail. Leaving that aside, I believe there is an important distinction between what might be called partisan influence and interference and political influence properly so termed. I believe as firmly as does any man that in any business matter with which we have to deal we should utterly divorce ourselves from any considerations of partisan complex. Party politics, feelings and influence, as distinct from political influence, are wholly bad when applied to public business. But that surely does not mean that this government and parliament shall totally abandon and abrogate all their influence, all their responsibility, in connection with a tremendous undertaking of this nature, one belonging to and to be managed and conserved in the interests of the Canadian people, the people whom this parliament represents, parliament to which the people look for the protection of their interests. Surely there is a wide distinction between partisanship, partisan interference, and a recognition of the vital and inescapable responsibility which must rest upon the administration and upon parliament in respect of any publicly owned and operated 
utility. As a matter of fact, while the Prime Minister emphasized the necessity of placing this board of trustees beyond the reach of political exigencies, of parliamentary influence, in almost the same breath he admitted and laid emphasis on the fact that in any circumstances, under the very terms of our constitution, the very terms on which any board of trustees must be appointed and money must be granted, the essential and fundamental responsibility of parliament must and shall be maintained. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Hants-Kings who preceded me. I believe we should make it very clear in legislation that ultimately the responsibility, the influence, the enacting of policies in the large, not the ordinary policies of management, but generally speaking the oversight of the policies of this country in respect of transportation matters, should be held, and if necessary, exercised by parliament. For, after all, we speak of the efficiency of certain men in carrying on a business of this character, and, as I suggested before, were that efficiency directed only towards one objective, were only one interest involved; were only one point of view affected; were only one objective sought, that of making the business financially sound, I would say that perhaps three, four or five efficient, honest, experienced business men might do better than has parliament at times. But that is not the only point. Transportation is so vital to every part of Canada, to every industry, that parliament cannot evade some responsibility as regards its general policies. For transportation may make or may damn a community; it may build an industry or destroy it; it may open up new territory or cause bankruptcy in and depopulate areas already settled. It may do almost anything. Next to finance, transportation is the lifeblood that makes industry, commerce, the life of the country, possible, and to my mind almost more than any other question it is one not only in which everyone is interested and vitally concerned, but in which parliament in the ultimate analysis must have the strongest and the final voice. For parliament cannot sit by and see any industry ruined, any part of the country depopulated by a body of business men, even though, in that depopulation and in that destruction, deficits are reduced and dividends paid.
But in my opinion there is one aspect that cannot and should not be forgotten. We speak of the solution of this great railway problem; we appoint commissions and we study and consider the question. We seek through legislation to remedy existing ills and to set the

system on its feet and make it financially sound. To my mind the transportation problem is caused by and inseparable from economic conditions as a whole throughout Canada, and it is no more possible to solve the transportation problem without dealing with it as part of a general policy of rehabilitation, and first removing the causes which have brought transportation into the position it now occupies, than it is to solve the problem of unemployment merely by tackling it as a problem by itself. Upon what is the problem based? There are two factors. Undoubtedly there was unwise expenditure, unnecessary competition, foolish duplication. All of those are assuredly factors. But what is the great and underlying factor? Why is it' that four short years ago this house and the country acclaimed every new loan and the president of this great company, the Canadian National Railways, was looked upon as the greatest man in Canada no matter what he spent; that he was encouraged, urged to spend more money because then times were prosperous and we looked to repay and more than repay all that had been expended? Now he has dropped into the shades of oblivion; the system is frowned upon, damned and indicted. Why? Because the freight which supports and makes profitable any system, upon which any system must depend, is lacking; because tonnage is cut in half or no longer found. You can no more solve the railway problem until you have adopted policies which will bring tonnage back; you can no more make the financial structure of the Canadian National sound and profitable until the condition of the people is improved, than you can remove unemployment without rehabilitating industry. The thing is impossible. To my mind one danger is that we ourselves shall look with too great optimism towards what might be done by any form of management, however high its degree of efficiency and its practice of stringent economy-that we shall look to see miracles performed. In the second place, the danger is that we shall go to the people of this country and say: "Lo, the railway problem is solved, the legislation is passed, the foundation is laid for prosperity and future progress for our transportation system," when we know in our hearts, and should never let the people forget, that whittle where you like, manage the system as efficiently as archangels could, it will not prosper until the people of Canada are prosperous. The system is just part of one great whole; and that is the culminating thought which I should like to leave upon the mind of the house. It is a part, an important part, but only a part in this general problem of economic depression
which now faces us, and the danger is, and it is a danger against which we must guard, that in this surge of enthusiasm, this determination regardless of all consequences and of every condition to make the system finnancially sound, we may do far more harm than good, we may so cut and mangle and destroy essential services that rehabilitation may be delayed or rendered impossible. I think that is one thing, Mr. Speaker, to which we must pay the greatest heed; for the saving of a few million dollars a year at the expense of deepening the depression in industry and agriculture would be a saving dearly bought, one which in the years to come might cost us fifty times the saving thereby accomplished. Reasonable economy, yes; reasonable cooperation, yes; but in our financial zeal do not let us forget that the primary function of a transportation system is to serve the communities of this country and to make possible the interchange of commodities between one industry and another. May I say, in conclusion, that, endeavouring as I have to deal only with principles, I have indicated that I approve of maintaining the present integrity of the national system, that I approve of a more efficient form of management, and I believe that the trustee form will be more efficient.
