The bill now before the house is based upon the report of the Duff commission. Enough already has been said about the constitution of that commission, the work it did, and the report it presented; I shall therefore not occupy the time of the house by reiterating what has been said in that respect. I have given the report a great deal of study and thought, and after stripping it bare and divesting it of all the frills, I find that three outstanding facts remain and refuse to be set aside.
The first fact is that we must always have railways in Canada. Geography itself says so. Our wide open spaces, the long distances, and the heavy commodities of farm and mine and forest, which can be moved only by rail transportation, make it necessary that we always have railways in this country.
The second fact is that motor transportation has come to stay, and it must be dealt with as such.
Third, and I am free to admit the most important fact of all, is that the taxpayers of Canada cannot long continue to pay every Saturday night a deficit of a million dollars on the Canadian National Railways.
The bill that is before the house is an attempt, I take it, to coordinate and amalgamate and bring together into one scheme the three facts which I have just mentioned. Just before I left Prince Edward Island to attend the present session of parliament I was asked to address a meeting of the railway employees of the city of Charlottetown. They were gathered together in their hall, and I received very short notice. I had no knowledge of the object of the meeting, nor did I know upon what subject I was expected to address them, but as the meeting opened this piece of paper was put in my hand, from which, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote a brief paragraph which sets forth what I conceive to be a worthy object on the part of the railway employees:
It is the object of this Traffic Club to unite all the employees and retired members on the island division of the Canadian National Railways, that they may work together and be of valuable assistance to the railway in its struggle to regain and retain its lost traffic from the various kinds of motor vehicles that have by means of very unfair competition made such inroads on its revenue. Transportation being the only goods we have to offer, it is our desire that we give same at a reasonable rate together with best possible service an up-to-date transportation company composed of a loyal bunch of workers can give.

In ather words, transportation is what we have to sell; let us go out and sell it. That was the object of the meeting of railway workers in the city of Charlottetown the day before I left home. I want to say for them, and I presume I am speaking for all railway workers throughout Canada, that they are absolutely loyal to the railways; their heart and soul is in their work, and, as is characteristic of railway men wherever you meet them, they hate the motor truck. It was their object to endeavour to secure for the railways that business which had been lost. In rising to address that meeting I prefaced my remarks by stating I had certain things to say to them with which I did not expect them to agree. By reason of the high duty on potatoes going into the United States, and because the Cuban market was closed to our products, we were forced to look elsewhere for our market. That market we found in central Canada, Ontario and Quebec. When we began to look around for means to move our crop to the Canadian market we found out, due to the fact that potatoes were very cheap, and that the consumer owing to curtailed buying power was not in a position to pay a high price for our commodity, that if we were to live at all it was necessary for us to get those potatoes to the market in the very cheapest possible way. The freight rate by rail on potatoes moving from Prince Edward Island to Montreal is thirty cents per hundred pounds, thirty-three cents to Ottawa and thirty-eight cents to Toronto. But we found last fall that by using steamships we were able to move our potatoes to the market in central Canada for about twenty cents per hundred pounds. For the first time in the history of my section of the country steamers left Prince Edward Island and proceeded up the St. Lawrence river to Montreal and Toronto. I should like hon. members to know that that is neither a popular nor a profitable way of transporting potatoes. Neither would it be at all necessary for the railways to meet the waterborne freight rate. The farmer or the shipper likes very much to have a railway car pull into his siding so that he may pile in his 500 sacks or 650 bushels, which go to make up the carload of potatoes. He likes to pile them in, neatly and snugly, close the doors and send the car through to its destination. At that time of the year those potatoes will leave the car in exactly the condition in which they went in.
That is not the case with potatoes carried by steamship. In the steamship there are from 40,000 to 60,000 sacks, and hon. members will readily understand that in loading, unloading and storing a cargo of that size some damage must result. Many potatoes are bruised, and a great deal of damage takes place. In my opinion by a very slight concession or a slight reduction in the rate for
the time being the railways would have had no difficulty in securing a twenty per cent increase in freight handled, and our section of the country would have been put in a much better condition.
I should like to say a word concerning the manner in which shippers and farmers are treated when they load cars. If a shipper is loading a steamer for Cuba, the railway company will allow him the use of cars for ten days. That is, cargoes may be assembled from the different railroad stations throughout the province and brought to the seaport. Under these circumstances no demurrage is charged during a ten day period. But for some reason which I cannot understand, and which I doubt whether any other hon. member can understand, when we seek to ship potatoes either to the United States or to another part of Canada, we are allowed the use of the cars for only five days. The assembling of a large cargo of potatoes consisting of 50,000 or 60,000 sacks requires a great number of cars and takes considerable time. A -steamer is not like a railway train; it does not always arrive at its destination at the time expected. Storm or accident of some kind may intervene, and it may be one, two or three days late, but only five days' use of the cars is permitted. Last fall our shippers sent a delegation to the head office of the Atlantic division at Moncton to ask that they be allowed ten days' use of the cars in loading steamers, but they were met with a blank refusal. If the general manager, Mr. Appleton, had been home at the time I think their request would have been successful, because we have always found him very obliging and willing to meet our wishes. However, he was not there, and this delegation met the freight or traffic manager who gave them a blank refusal, The result was that the shippers had to unload their cars into the freight sheds, which entailed a second handling at extra expense and with additional damage to potatoes. Some of the shippers were so vexed about the matter that they moved their potatoes to the seaport by motor truck instead of using the railway.

am democratic and I do not believe in taxation without representation. He must have the ability to save money; he must have due regard for economy on all occasions, but above that there is one other qualification which to my mind is more essential, and that is his ability to go out and get business. Transportation is the only commodity he will have to sell; let him go out and sell it, not according to any rigid, cast-iron classification rules but in the way that will be easiest and most beneficial to the patrons of the railway.

means,-that the privately owned railroad is going to be hamstrung. The value of their assets will decrease as soon as this legislation goes on the statute book. Why? Because when a dispute arises the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways each appoints an arbitrator on the arbitral tribunal, the chairman of the railway commission acting as the third. We will suppose that the chairman decides in favour of the Canadian National Railways. In that event is the Canadian Pacific Railway going to be favourably disposed towards the Canadian National Railways? Or if in another case the decision is given in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway, is Mr. Hungerford or are those men in charge of the national railways going to feel kindly towards the other line? We will not effect economies if we have the railways at each others throats,-and that is exactly what will happen when the arbitral tribunal is operating.
If we are to have economies we must have voluntary cooperation between the two railways. Nobody can convince me in this day and generation, after the experiences of the last few years, that this legislation is necessary, so far as economies are concerned. There is no doubt there were extravagances on the part of both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National; we all admit it and know it in our own experience and business. In his speech on Tuesday the Minister of Railways bore me out when he told us how much money was saved in the last year. If these economies were put into effect and these large sums of money were saved without the operation of a compulsory arbitral tribunal, surely Mr. Beatty and his directors and shareholders will make sure that he cooperates with the Canadian National Railways, without having to be forced to do it by legislation.
I say economies would take place more quickly and with less difficulty if the railways were left alone, on the one hand the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway watching Mr. Beatty and his directors, and on the other hand the people of Canada represented by their members in this House of Commons watching the management of the Canadian National Railways. That is the only way we will ever have proper cooperation, and because of that I say this bill is unnecessary, that it interferes with private rights and is not in the best interests either of Canada or the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway. For that reason I purpose voting against it.

Mr. Speaker, we are requested to consider a measure which, according to the hon. Minister of Railways, is based on the conclusion of the Duff commission. There is, therefore, reason to believe that the report will serve as a guide to the new management of our National railways.
The object which the royal commission, composed of seven members, appointed by the government on November 20, 1931, had in view, was to study the difficult situation in which our National railways are placed, discover the causes and find a remedy.
The work carried out by the commissioners is certainly one of the most thorough and praiseworthy which has ever been presented to parliament. They discovered the main sources of the evil and made the most commendable suggestions, that cannot be gainsaid. However, the true remedy has not been pointed out; perhaps, they thought it was better not to mention it at present, and certain recommendations made therefore, seem to be in contradiction with the principles of economic management.
Numerous factors, it is stated, have contributed to create the sad plight of our National railways; first, the extensive mileage in contrast with our population, trade depression, competition by the Canadian Pacific railway and the various other transportation facilities such as motor trucks, autobus, aeroplanes and ships; the high rates charged on freight and passenger traffic, and the high cost of labour. All the commissioners, however, agree in asserting that one of the main causes was the acquisition of railways and ancillary lines, most of them bankrupt, necessitating very large disbursements in interest and fixed charges. Additional causes were repairs to the railways which had deteriorated and had been neglected, in many instances, requiring a complete rebuilding of both the roadway and stations, so as to put them in condition to meet competition by the Canadian Pacific railway; the erection of hotels, still to meet competition, the establishment of maritime services, always with the same end in view, and finally, an overstaffed management drawing too high salaries. To remedy the first evil, the report recommends abolishing the duplication of train services, both railways to cooperate in this respect. This is an excellent recommendation, this useless war was carried on to the detriment of the two railways, moreover, the public could be given an efficient service without this duplication. By discontinuing to operate the unnecessary lines, instead of having 95 53719-183J
per cent of lines in use there would only be 58 per cent; the operating cost, maintenance and wear and tear would greatly be lessened; therefore, the saving would be very appreciable.
The report, moreover, recommends the merger of the telegraph and express services. This suggestion is an excellent one and a further saving would result.
The maritime coastal service of the Canadian National Railway between Vancouver, Victoria and Seattle, undertaken at a great loss, should be entirely discontinued. The extravagant hotel system should be leased, for it is out of proportion to the requirements of the population.
While recognizing the service rendered by motor trucks and autobus, a service with which the railways cannot compete, owing to its particular facilities, and which better highways has developed and will further develop, the commissioners are of the opinion that it would only be fair to fix minimum rates for the conveyance of goods by railways and motor trucks, so as to establish a workable system between these various conveyances.
This is a recommendation with which I do not entirely agree, and I do not think it is of a nature to improve the situation. First, the question relating to motor vehicles comes entirely under the jurisdiction of the provinces which issue the licences, collect the taxes and establish regulations for the safety and maintenance of their highways. This service is already highly assessed and cannot stand any further taxation), especially, in times of crisis when we are aware that the special advantages derived from this kind of transportation cannot be duplicated by railways.
This recommendation, to my mind, is unfair to the public. It would not matter were the two systems of transportation identical; however, under present circumstances, it means charging the public a higher price, equivalent to that of railways, an antiquated system of conveyance which has seen better days; it means impeding progress which modern methods demand.

To my mind, the representatives of the people cannot ignore this fact entirely. Therefore although agreeing that the management of our railways should be carried on in a business way, it is

The royal commission is not opposed to the St. Lawrence deep waterways, it contends that this undertaking will not harm railway traffic. Quite the contrary, common sense tells us that the dredging of a deep water route to the head of the Great lakes will considerably decrease the railway traffic, owing to lower transportation rates although this method of conveyance is slower. Take, for instance, an ocean ship loaded at any European port, bound for Fort William, instead of Montreal, the cargo thus shipped will mean so much freight taken away from the railways between the two last mentioned points, there is no avoiding this fact. Notwithstanding the outlay of millions of dollars to construct this deep waterway, ships being exempt from taxation, this water route becomes a conveyance subsidized by the State, by those who, themselves, are endeavouring to extricate their railways from the sad plight in which it has fallen, by subsidizing a great rival to aggravate its plight-this seems most absurd.
The report further expresses the views that the wheat increase in the west-although the shipping is to the Pacific ocean and then via the Panama canal or else to Churchill- will always leave a tonnage equal to that of to-day to be shipped East, via Montreal and the Atlantic ocean. Increased wheat production, at present, is very uncertain. In fact, in normal times, such should be the case, and the western prairies could feed a greater proportion of the world's population. However, the contrary is happening at present. This wheat increase is precisely taking place in countries which in the past imported our wheat; however, as long as the world's policy remains unchanged, Canada has very little chance of exporting more wheat.
The commission suggests as a remedy, at Chapter V, Section 204, the appointment of three trustees to see that their recommendations are put into practice. A majority of the trustees should rule, but the majority's decisions would depend on the good pleasure of the chairman. For the purpose of settling disputes it suggests-Section 213-the appointment of the Chief Commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners and a representative of the two companies concerned. When decisions cannot be arrived at on important matters the exchequer court would be empowered to appoint two additional trustees. Section 213 is as follows:
Where the execution of an order involves the doing of any act which by an existing statute requires the assent or approval of the

Board of Railway Commissioners or where in the opinion of the Chief Commissioner himself the public interests involved are of sufficient importance to warrant it. no order made by the arbitral tribunal shall be operative without the concurrence of the Chief Commissioner and his formal written assent.
It is clearly shown that the members of this arbitral tribunal and trustees amount to placing the control of all railways in the hands of one man, the Chairman of the Railway Commission, which seems most arbitrary. It is an absolute dictatorship. If, in the appointment of this arbitral tribunal, there was only a question of the interests of the National Railways involved, the granting of such wide powers would certainly be a dangerous proceeding, but where it takes a more serious meaning, is when it violates the contract entered into, in 1881, between the Dominion government and the C.P.R. in which it is stipulated that the Pacific company will manage, maintain and operate its railways and properties, itself, perpetually. If we consider that 35,000 Canadians are shareholders in this company, that they have invested money well earned and savings realized by hard work, while being also taxed to maintain the C.N.R. and that they have put up their own money in purchasing this private railway, it would certainly 'be unjust to dispossess them to-day of their property either directly or indirectly, by placing this private enterprise under the management of this arbitral tribunal, in conjunction with the Canadian National Railway. All seem to point that the state would have the right to ruin a prosperous and indispensible company to save another from bankruptcy. The arbitral tribunal would, perhaps, be acceptable if its powers were limited to controlling the expenditure of the Canadian National Railway and regulating all unreasonable competition between the two systems.
When prosperity prevailed throughout Canada between 1896 and 1911, the future of the country appeared so promising that governments had grounds to venture into railway enterprises, either by means of subsidizing or undertaking the work themselves. They had the means at their disposal and it was but natural to first build railways to transport, afterwards, the pioneers of the country. Railways have alwas's been the means of establishing and developing new settlements. The credit of settling the western provinces must be given to the railways. Without their initiative all these beautiful regions would still be inhabited only by the Indian tribes, scattered here and there. The transcontinental lines made confederation what it is

to-day. Even then the thought of calling the western plains the granary of the empire and visions of feeding part of Europe existed. Immigration at that period increased our population without hindering anyone. Nobody foresaw this terrible war of 1914, which was in a few years to transform our country, blot out our prosperity, jeopardize our enterprises and trade, and imperil our credit. The world crisis began to spread over the land. This scourge, known as war, upset everything not only among us but throughout the world. To-day, nations impoverished seek to produce their own food. We witnessed foreign countries which in the past had sought our exports, become self-supporting and even invade our own markets. All nations vied with one another in erecting tariff barriers. Canada with its untold natural resources, with a population of hardly 10,000,000 souls is overtaxed and crippled with debts, its people are inactive although the country overflows with produets. The royal commission appointed to solve one of our great problems has failed in its task; its recommendations will in no way better our lot, because the problem to be solved is far greater than that of our railways. The commissioners perhaps visualized the real remedy; however, in this period of trade stagnation and universal unemployment, they dared not make it known for fear of further jeopardizing our situation as a whole; perhaps they thought, not without cause, that their recommendations would not be welcomed by the public, seeing that 500,000 men were unemployed, and at a time when the producer cannot find a purchaser, owing to our impoverished state.
We had reason to expect that this commission, after scrutinizing and analyzing the affairs of our national railway would have visited other countries where there were also railway problems, in order to study on the spot the means adopted to solve these problems and be in a position to recommend to the government a measure differing from that now submitted to us. At all events, the legislation which we are now considering can only be at the most a temporary remedy and not a cure to our railway ills. As I have shown, this measure tends to be unjust, arbitrary and liable to aggravate a more serious problem, that of unemployment, if we examine what other countries have done for their railways we find that they have not followed our example, they have not lost their time in shifting their ills. France, which had to bear the brunt of the Great war, finding the financial situation of her railways threatened, adopted as a remedy
the immediate electrification of her vast system, Paris-Lyon-Mediterranee et Orleans-Midi. The Swiss confederation electrified with success her entire railway system. Our neighbours, the United States, whose water powers are not to be compared with those of Canada, did not hesitate to electrify their Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul, Butte, Anaconda, Pacific railway system and others.
Some time ago the press informed us that an Anglo-Franco-German syndicate, with a capital of $580,000,000, had been formed to electrify the railways of Poland, Rumania, Iraq and Portugal which were threatened with bankruptcy. In Canada, with a surplus of water powers-for with only 3 per cent of our railways electrified and our financial situation not in a worse state than that of those countries-the government has no better measure to offer us than this inadequate legislation. It may be contended that the cost of establishing such a system would be very high. If in other countries such a transformation has been carried out everywhere with success, under no better conditions than those prevailing here, why should Canada refuse to follow their example? Since Canada is undeniably in a more favourable situation, any opposition to such a scheme can only arise from certain groups which are interested in blocking such a progressive move. According to statements published by the Butte-Anaconda Railway, we are able to state that for one year's operations-all expenditures included-with a capital of $1,200,000, that company realized a profit of $242,000. When it is known that the Chicago-Mil-waukee and St. Paul system comprising 440 miles, a distance equal to that from Ottawa to New York, which, to-day, however, extends over 600 miles, cost $12,500,000, out of this amount the actual cost of 112 locomotives transferred to other lines must be deducted, we are amazed to hear that one hesitates over a few millions of dollars to provide the country with the only system capable of competing advantageously against all other systems of conveyance. Each year, we face, without flinching, the enormous deficits of our railways, although we are aware of the great advantages of the electrified locomotive such as traction, braking power, etc., over the steam locomotive, and the small operating cost entailed compared with the steam system.
